1	- Twyne UX improvement brief
2	- Discussion notes and proposed product directionKeith Noel • October 19, 2026
3	- Twyne needs to make its editorial work visible, explain why its feedback matters, and connect that feedback to the passages a writer can act on. This brief consolidates the observations and suggestions from our discussion about cast replies, passage relationships, editor reviews, automatic research, and manuscript versions.
4	- The guiding principle is that every card should help the writer make a recognizable writing decision. Prioritize reliable delivery of review and research results, then develop richer passage and revision views.
5	- What was observed
6	- Cast or persona response cards sometimes quote several manuscript passages, but currently appear to link only to one region or the initial quotation.
7	- A visually appealing view connects passages A and B without clearly explaining why they are connected or what the writer should do with that relationship. The exact name and purpose of the “further on as you read” card remain uncertain.
8	- Editor feedback requested from the rubric initially appeared absent. Later in the same session, responses did appear, but discovering them required a manual click. This changes the diagnosis: delivery and visibility are established concerns; a generation failure was not established.
9	- The apparatus or automatic research area appeared to remain at “watching graph,” without visible research findings. This does not establish whether background research actually ran.
10	- Manual checks appeared to run, although the tools felt inconsistent. The editorial board version page offered checkpoint restoration and revision tasks, but its words and passages before-and-after bars did not communicate useful revision insight.
11	- How to read this brief
12	- Observations reflect the walkthrough, not an independent code or runtime audit. Proposed behavior captures the improvements discussed. Completion criteria below translate those proposals into reviewable outcomes; they are not claims about implemented functionality. “Jev” refers to the type-safe System One decision model or system, including the transcription variants GEV and Jeb.
13	- Passage links and meaningful feedback
14	- Link every quotation to its source
15	- Each quoted manuscript passage inside a cast reply should have its own connection to the corresponding source passage. A response discussing several passages must support several links, rather than sending every quotation to the first anchor.
16	- The discussion began with Jev identifying quotations in the response, then moved toward deterministic matching because literal quotations should already exist in the manuscript. Use direct text matching where possible. Model judgment is useful when interpretation is needed, but is unnecessary for an unambiguous exact quote.
17	- Make each resolved quote clickable. Activating it should jump to and highlight its own manuscript passage.
18	- Use surrounding context to distinguish repeated phrases. Matching the same words in two places is not enough to identify the intended source.
19	- As an implementation safeguard, leave uncertain or unmatched quotations unresolved rather than silently assigning an incorrect passage. Revalidate links when edits change the source text.
20	- Explain why passages are related
21	- Preserve the useful visual connection between passages, but add a plain explanation of the relationship and its writing consequence. Showing two excerpts alone leaves the writer to infer the purpose of the card.
22	- Possible relationship labels discussed were an unpaid promise, a conflict, or an echo. Pair the label with a specific explanation: for example, an earlier passage introduces an expectation that the later passage has not yet addressed. These are illustrative categories, not confirmed names of current features.
23	- Show why these particular passages were selected and what question or revision the connection raises.
24	- Let the writer agree with the interpretation or push back. A relationship is an editorial reading, not automatically a defect.
25	- Inspect the existing “further on as you read” feature before deciding whether its presentation, name, or underlying function needs to change.
26	- Protect author intent and remember decisions
27	- Let writers tell the editors what they intend to preserve, so feedback does not erase an intentional stylistic or structural choice. Give feedback memory: the writer should be able to mark a note “intentional” or “later” and avoid receiving the same note repeatedly unless the relevant text changes.
28	- Completion criteria
29	- A response containing three distinct quotations can navigate to all three intended passages. Repeated phrases do not silently point to the wrong occurrence. Each relationship card explains its editorial relevance, and dismissed or deferred feedback respects the writer’s recorded decision.
30	- Editor reviews and automatic research
31	- Make requested reviews visible
32	- The later appearance of editor replies is a crucial correction to the initial report of no response. The immediate issue is that the writer could not tell what was happening and had to click to uncover the result. Investigate generation timing separately from notification and display behavior.
33	- After a review request, show that reviewing is in progress. When it finishes, clearly show that feedback is ready and identify the editor speaking.
34	- If the writer remains in the relevant panel, display the returned feedback automatically. If the writer moves away, use a quiet unread indicator that leads directly to it.
35	- As a completion safeguard, distinguish a finished review with no findings from a pending review or an error; none should look like unexplained silence.
36	- Give Jev a clear editorial role
37	- Jev should help decide when proactive reviews are useful and which editor is relevant to the current text or situation. The walkthrough did not make this selection behavior apparent. The proposed separation is to use Jev for relevance and prioritization while treating delivery of explicitly requested feedback as dependable application behavior.
38	- This means the writer should be able to understand who is responding and why that editor is useful. A requested review should not remain hidden merely because a separate prioritization decision has not surfaced it.
39	- Make automatic research produce an outcome
40	- The apparatus felt severely underdeveloped because “watching graph” did not lead to visible findings. The next investigation should determine whether the missing outcome comes from triggering, execution, or presentation. The discussion does not establish which layer is responsible.
41	- Center the research experience on a claim in the manuscript. Show sources that support it, challenge it, or leave it unresolved, and explain what that evidence means for the wording or credibility of the passage. The writer needs findings or a clear reason that no useful result is available.
42	- Connect research findings back to the claim or passage that prompted them.
43	- Make the current state understandable: watching for relevant claims, researching, findings ready, or no useful result. Expose failures as actionable states rather than leaving the display at “watching graph.”
44	- Treat the observation that manual checks run as a useful diagnostic lead, not proof that the automatic research path works.
45	- Completion criteria
46	- A requested editor review becomes visible without a discovery click when its panel is open, and has an unread indication when closed. Automatic research yields a claim-linked finding or an intelligible explanation of its outcome. A writer can distinguish waiting, completion, and failure.
47	- Versions and delivery priorities
48	- Organize versions around revision intent
49	- The version page should help the writer understand what changed and decide whether the revision served its purpose. Word and passage totals can remain secondary metadata, but bars displaying counts alone do not explain the value or effect of an edit.
50	- Lead with meaningful changes such as an opening rewritten, an argument moved, or a scene cut. Let the writer open the actual before-and-after passages for each change. These examples illustrate the desired level of explanation; they are not observed changes in a specific manuscript.
51	- Keep checkpoint restoration available and easy to understand.
52	- Visualize substantive revision information when it has actually been captured, instead of presenting counts as the main insight.
53	- Connect revision tasks to the editor suggestions they address. Add a brief assessment of how the revision responds to the suggestion, while leaving the final judgment to the writer.
54	- Make it possible to inspect the textual evidence behind any change summary or assessment.
55	- Completion criteria
56	- Given two checkpoints, the writer can identify a meaningful revision, inspect the corresponding before-and-after text, and understand its relationship to an editorial task where one exists. Restoration remains accessible. Counts provide context without dominating the page.
57	- Proposed order of work
58	- 1. Stabilize editor feedback delivery and automatic research outcomes. First make the application clearly return useful work, explain its state, and expose the difference between no result and a failed operation.
59	- 2. Improve passage grounding and card meaning. Resolve every quotation, explain passage relationships, and make feedback respond to author intent and recorded decisions.
60	- 3. Develop the richer version experience. Build on reliable passage links and feedback to explain revisions, show evidence, and connect changes to editorial goals.
61	- Questions to resolve during implementation
62	- What are the exact component names and intended purposes of the cast cards and the “further on as you read” view?
63	- Did the editor review finish before the manual click, or did that click initiate or refresh the result? What state was visible while waiting?
64	- What triggers automatic research, and where does the path stop when only “watching graph” is shown?
65	- Which editor-selection and review-timing decisions are already made by Jev, and how are those decisions surfaced?
66	- What revision information is currently captured beyond word and passage counts, and can it support trustworthy explanations of changes?
67

content.text:
I've worked through all three parts of the brief in its suggested order. Typecheck and lint are clean, and the 129 tests in the files I touched pass (16 of them new). I haven't run the full test suite or checked any of this in the browser. Nothing is committed.

## 1. Editor feedback and research now report what's happening
- **Editor review in the rubric:** the Editors tab used to show "0" after a quick grade. That looked like the feedback was missing, but the quick check never asks the editors at all. The tab now says "not asked", or "reading…" while a run is in progress, and the empty panel explains why. This answers the brief's question about the manual click: the click *started* the review, nothing had been waiting.
- **Research no longer just says "watching":** the research module went quietly idle in five different situations. It now records which one and shows a plain sentence for it in both the side panel and the Apparatus page:
  - the draft is too short
  - no AI provider is set
  - it found no claims needing a source
  - every claim is already covered
  - the pass finished
- **Each research claim** now says what its result means. "No match" means the search ran and found nothing. "Failed" means the search broke, which is different from an empty result, and can be retried. Each claim also has a "Go to the claim" link.

## 2. Quotes link to their passages, and cards explain themselves
- **Every quote in an editor's note is clickable** (`src/utils/quote-grounding.ts`). This works in the note itself, in replies, and in the note that opens inside the manuscript. Matching is plain text matching that ignores quote styles, case and spacing, and handles quotes with "…" cut out of them. When a phrase appears more than once, the words around the quote in the note pick which one; a tie stays unresolved. A quote that can't be placed gets a dotted underline that says why. Links are re-checked whenever the draft changes, and again at the moment of the click.
- **"Further on in this piece" cards** now name the relationship: unpaid promise, tension, echo, repetition or same subject. Each comes with a one-line explanation, a view of both passages, and two buttons: "That's the connection" and "Not how I read it". If Jev decides two passages only share vocabulary, the card isn't shown at all.
- **"Intentional" and "later" buttons on each note.** That editor won't raise the same passage again until its text changes. The decisions are also passed to the editors as context, and settled notes are shown faded.

## 3. Version history
- Each checkpoint can record what the revision was for, and that intent is shown alongside it.
- Changes are labelled "Rewritten", "Cut" or "New passage", with the before and after text.
- If a change rewrote a passage an editor had commented on, that note appears beside it. The wording says it touched the note, not that it answered it.
- Word and passage counts are now folded into a "Size of the change" section you can expand. Restore works as before.

## Not done, and things to check
- **Unread markers for finished reviews**, from the completion criteria, aren't built.
- **Relationship labels come from an extra Jev question** added to the existing echo check. Cards created before this change, or when Jev can't be reached, fall back to "Shared words" with an explanation that nothing has read them for meaning.
- **"Not how I read it" just hides the card** using the existing dismiss. Nothing records that reading as rejected.
- **"Intentional" and "later" decisions are saved only in this browser**, keyed per document. They don't sync to Convex.

A source-check test had the old rendering call hard-coded, so I updated `personas-markdown-wiring.test.ts` to match.

---
name: autonomy-by-default
description: Twyne should act on its own by default — reviews, research, editor readings run without the writer clicking; buttons are optional overrides
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Twyne's default is autonomous, fluid action: editors read, research runs, reviews complete, and results arrive without the writer having to press a button. Manual controls may exist as options (re-run, steer, decline), but a feature that waits for a click before doing its core job is a design defect.

**Why:** The user (Keith Noel's product direction, restated by the owner 2026-10-20) said "waiting for the user to click a button is not what I want for this app… the default is autonomous fluid action."

**How to apply:** When building or fixing a feature, ask "does this happen if the writer never clicks?" If not, add an automatic trigger (on draft change / idle / panel open / folio open) with spend guards (dedupe per draft fingerprint, rate floors, session caps) rather than a call-to-action button. Empty states should say what the app is about to do on its own, not invite a click. Hosted (non-BYOK) users must get the autonomous path too. Related: [[skip-long-verification]].

content.text:
Twyne's default is now to act on its own. Typecheck and lint are clean and the 125 tests in the touched files pass (including 6 new ones). I haven't run the full suite or watched any of this happen in the browser, and nothing is committed.

## What now happens without a click

- **Editors read a draft as soon as it opens.** Before, any text already in a document counted as "already read", so the editors never commented on a draft until you clicked Get notes. Now Twyne remembers, per document, what the editors last read. A document they've never seen is read on its own once it reaches 500 words and you pause. Documents that already have notes stay quiet when reopened.
- **Rewrites trigger a reading, not just new text.** It used to take 500 *net new* words plus a 2-minute pause, so tightening or reworking prose never woke the editors. Now 200 new or rewritten words plus a 1-minute pause triggers a reading. The existing limits stay: at least 5 minutes between readings and at most 8 per session.
- **Research works without your own AI model.** Before, a signed-in writer with no model configured got no automatic research at all. Now Twyne picks out likely claims from the text itself (figures, quotations, "studies show", dated events), Jev confirms which really need a source, and the search runs through Twyne's service. Fiction is handled differently, so made-up events don't get researched. This is in `src/utils/research-candidates.ts`.
- **Failed research retries itself.** A failed pass or claim is tried again after 30 seconds, then 2 minutes, then 10 minutes. After that it stops and the retry button stays on screen.
- **The editors' reading in the rubric runs on its own.** When a new quick grade arrives for a version the editors haven't read, they read it in the background, at most every 10 minutes, and the grade stays visible meanwhile. Their notes no longer disappear when the next quick grade refreshes. If you keep typing during their reading, the notes are kept and marked as being on an earlier version.
- **Versions describe themselves.** Every comparison now gets a sentence like "Rewrote 3 passages and cut 1. The changes reach passages Marrow had notes on." The "what was this revision for" field is now optional.

The buttons are all still there (Get notes, Ask them now, Grade this draft, retry), but as shortcuts. Empty panels now say what Twyne is about to do instead of asking you to click. I updated the in-app manual's two passages about asking the editors to match.

## Decisions for you

- **Cost.** These changes spend more model calls than before. Editors can read up to 8 times per session, the rubric reading up to 6 times an hour, and hosted research makes one batched Jev call per pass. The limits are constants in `background-room.ts`, `rubric-panel.tsx` (`ROOM_READ_FLOOR_MS`) and `background-research.ts`.
- **Automatic rubric readings save versions less often.** A reading you ask for still always saves a checkpoint. One the editors start themselves follows the same 5-minute spacing as automatic checkpoints, so they can't push your own checkpoints out of the 50-version history.
- **Some things deliberately stay manual:** inserting citations into the manuscript, Propose edits, and the full-page analysis. These either change your text or are a deeper on-demand view.

I also saved "autonomous by default" as a standing preference for future work on Twyne.

A guide to using the writing room, understanding its data, and maintaining the app.

**For writers:** open [The Manual](https://www.twyne.love/docs/) in Twyne. It covers
the desk, the House, conversations in the margin, source and proof, and shortcuts.
Numbered visual walkthroughs show the actual controls, with editor illustrations
and optional films at the beginning of relevant chapters. The contents panel
follows your current chapter and shows your reading position as you scroll.

**For contributors:** start with the [project README](../README.md#development),
then follow the guide for the part you are changing.

## The writing room

| Guide                                                 | Use it for                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

| [Live voice](live-voice.md)                           | Voice sessions, the relay and conversation limits.                                  |
| [Publishing from Twyne](publishing-from-twyne.md)     | Writer-owned PDS publishing and public reading pages.                               |
| [Not Organic identity](notorganic-native-identity.md) | The account boundary and native sign-in design.                                     |
| [Launch film](launch-film.md)                         | The bilingual introduction, contextual chapter films and visual walkthrough assets. |

## Running and maintaining Twyne

| Guide                                                       | Use it for                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |

| [Data and sync architecture](architecture/data-and-sync.md) | The recorded storage/sync architecture and its dated findings. |

| [AI observability](ai-observability.md)                     | Traces, experiments and editorial evaluation.                  |
| [Popmelt integration](popmelt.md)                           | The recorded capture and interaction integration.              |

## Design and implementation records

These describe intent and implementation history. A plan is not evidence that a
feature is deployed or that its provider integration has been exercised.

| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |

that draft, Salt Roads, from a brief to a proof.

Twyne is a writing desk with an editorial room attached. You write on the page. A small cast of editors reads in the margin, each with a different job, and nothing they say changes a word until you say so. Three habits make the room worth having:

  1. Say what the piece is for. The{" "} dossier holds the reader, the goal and the shape of the piece. Editors with a brief give better notes than editors guessing.
  2. Write first, read notes later. Your draft saves on this device as you type.{" "} The margin holds feedback beside the passage it belongs to, and waits until you look up.
  3. Revise on your own terms. Follow a note to its passage, argue with it, ask a different editor, or check the galley proof. Every change is yours to make or refuse.

Go to the writing desk →

02 · At the desk

The dossier

Morgan's first draft of Salt Roads was beautiful and pointless. The dossier is where you admit what a piece is supposed to do, so the editors can tell you whether it does it.

Before the room opens, it asks a short series of questions. They feel like paperwork and they are the opposite: a dossier is the difference between an editor saying "this paragraph is weak" and an editor saying "this paragraph loses the reader you said you were writing for." Answer briefly and honestly. You can change any answer later.

Ten sections, and what each is really asking:

  • Working title. A name the room can use. It does not have to be the final one.
  • Form. Essay, memo, chapter, dispatch, proposal. The shape sets expectations about length and

04 · At the desk

Writing in flow

Morgan writes in long runs and resents anything that interrupts one. The room is built to wait.

While you work, Twyne can bring comments, sources, books, records and echoes of your earlier writing into the margin, each beside the passage it concerns. Nothing pops up over the page. Hover or focus a marker to see what it connects to; select it to open the conversation in the same margin.

A quieter page

Automatic focus reads your typing cadence. When you have been writing steadily for a while, it quiets the room: new cards wait, controls recede, and the page is the only thing left. Pause, or reach for the room, and it comes back. You can also enter focus yourself with Zen in the manuscript status bar, and leave it with Esc.

Help when you need it

When a passage stalls, the margin may offer a single connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are offers, not corrections; ignore them and they go away. If what you are writing drifts from the dossier, the room may propose an amendment. It never rewrites the brief behind your back.

Your controls: Automatic review, margin tools, automatic focus and cover lookups each have their own switch in the review controls. The desk learns your timing and preferences on this device. Cover lookups are the one feature here that talks to the outside world: they send book or record titles to external catalogues.

05 · At the desk

The piece

Some problems only show up across the whole draft: the voice that shifts, the name spelled two ways, the character who vanishes for a chapter.

Useful without a model

The piece runs on this device, with no model and no cost. It watches first-person stance, similar names, and the conventions your draft mostly follows: spelling, small numbers, quotation marks, dashes and list punctuation. It also maps where each recurring name appears across the headed sections. A finding is a pattern worth a look. Whether it is a problem is your call.

Choose Stance, Names, Style or Presence to see that lens on the page. Open a finding for its passages and the actions it offers. On a narrow screen the desk sits below the writing area, and Close gives the space back to the draft. Zen hides it while you write.

Know what the score means

The ≈ sign marks an estimate. Consistency can move as you revise, because local rules re-count; that movement is not a new editorial opinion. Score details separates the measures made by rule from those made by review. An overall estimate appears at about 150 words.

Confirm with a full read asks for a fresh editorial reading of the current draft. It needs automatic review switched on, at least 500 words, and a signed-in model service. The desk says so when a request cannot run. Edit again afterwards and the score becomes an estimate until the new draft has been read.

Your choices stay yours. Fixes change only the listed passages, and Undo reverses them. A deliberate exception stays with the folio on this device. Above 80,000 characters the desk pauses these checks and asks you to divide the work into folios.

06 · At the desk

Writing instruments

A sentence that is almost right. A paragraph that sounds like one you wrote earlier. A scene with no sound in it. Each gets a tool that opens beside the words, not instead of them.

Select text in the manuscript and the tools that fit it appear. A single word offers Alternatives. A passage offers Rework, with Hear it read, Threads, Scene bench and Task desk under More. The Compositor also opens Task desk from Review. Close a tool, or press Escape, and the page is back.

content.content:
07 · The editorial room

Your editors

Five resident voices, each reading for something different. No single editor is right about everything, which is rather the point of having five.

You will come to know them by their faces. The same portraits accompany each editor's critiques, margin replies and rubric readings, so a glance tells you whether it was the sceptic or the copy chief who objected. A custom editor without a portrait signs with their initials. From any writing instrument, Ask the room brings one of them into the question you are already working on.

Arrange your room

Custom editors: Visit{" "} the Room of Editors {" "} to add, edit or reorder the cast. An editor needs a name, a role and a description of how they talk; the more specific the description, the more consistently the model stays in character. Morgan's Route Reader exists because nobody else in the room cared about distances.

Changing the model

Each editor is only as good as the model reading for them. A careful, precise model makes Mlle. Sceptique sharper. A warmer one makes Sœur Encourageante more generous. In{" "} Preferences {" "} you can assign different models to different jobs, and the room adapts.

08 · The editorial room

The galley proof

Salt Roads got a B. That is not information. The reasons under the grade are.

The static features are the part of the proof that never guesses: sentence length distribution, type-token ratio, citation density, paragraph shape. They are computed on this device, cost nothing and call nothing. They give you a cold, honest picture of the draft's mechanics, and nothing at all about whether it is any good.

Quick check

When the signed-in service is available, the default check makes one typed judgement request against your enabled criteria, custom ones included. You get a grade without separate verdicts from the five editors. If the quick check is unavailable, Twyne falls back to the room reading.

The editors' reading

After a quick check, the editors read the new version on their own, at most once every ten minutes, and the grade stays on screen while they do. Choose Ask them now on the Editors tab if you would rather not wait. Each editor gives a score and a rationale, and the places where they disagree are usually where the revision is. This path combines editorial verdicts with the static features. Its Target Fit check caps the shape scores when a piece misses the audience or purpose in its dossier, because a beautifully built essay for the wrong reader is still the wrong essay.

What the letters mean:

  • A range. Publishable or nearly so. Polish.
  • B range. A solid draft with clear, fixable problems. This is where Salt Roads sits.
  • C range. Doing the work, but a real pass is still needed.
  • D to F range. The important next pass is still ahead.

Use the rationale, not the letter: read the explanation beside each criterion and hold it against your own purpose. The rubric is one more reading of the draft. You decide which of its complaints deserve a revision.

09 · The editorial room

Margin conversations

Every argument about a passage happens next to the passage. Your notes, the editors' notes, and the replies between them.

Select any passage and choose Comment to leave a note in the margin. Notes belong to the folio and travel with it. Each one can hold replies, and Ask an editor invites a particular voice into the thread when you want a second opinion on your own doubt.

Select a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve it there. One conversation is in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. A reply you have not sent survives switching threads during the visit, but not a reload, so send it or lose it.

10 · The editorial room

Research & citations

The 1911 survey, the tide table, the book Morgan keeps paraphrasing. The Apparatus notices them and keeps them in order.

The Apparatus does three things: finds sources, keeps them, and cites them. As you write it recognises DOIs, URLs, ISBNs and author-year references in the text. You can also search by query; the panel returns a shortlist with title, author, publisher and a snippet. Save what matters to the bibliography and ignore the rest.

The bibliography is formatted in the style you choose, MLA, APA or Chicago, and switches instantly when an editor changes their mind. Copy the whole list to the clipboard in one go.

The full Apparatus lives at{" "} /apparatus . The citation tab in the right panel shows a quick view of what has been detected without leaving the page.

import { WRITING_LENSES } from "../../../utils/writing-lenses"; import { component$ } from "@qwik.dev/core"; import { Link, type DocumentHead } from "@qwik.dev/router"; import { LegalPage } from "../../../components/legal/legal-page"; export default component$(() => (

Automatic review

When review is enabled, saved writing and relevant dossier information are sent to the configured AI service after a pause. Use the Automatic review switch in the Tools board to pause or resume review. Findings are suggestions; Twyne does not rewrite your draft.

Grades

The rubric grades your draft against its criteria. Open a criterion to read its reasoning, or open “How this was scored” for the calculation behind a grade. Grades are estimates to help you revise, not a verdict on your writing.

Writing checks

Jev runs these checks during automatic review when the required material is available, even with the Tools board closed. Open a check to inspect its latest reading. Choose different revisions or add a focus when you want to steer it, then use “Run this check”. Audience changes and edits to

13 · Your work

Folios, export & publishing

One piece per folio. Salt Roads, its outline and a scratch file of cut paragraphs share a collection and nothing else.

Folios are separate documents with separate dossiers. Switch between them from the drawer. Each keeps its own word count, last-updated time and, if you want, its own layout settings.

Export a folio as Markdown, standalone HTML, plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup: a JSON file with the brief, the folios and their content. All of it is under File in the masthead.

Share publishes a public reading view of a folio. Anyone with the link can read it and nobody can edit it. Unpublish takes it down at once.

Publish to your PDS by connecting Bluesky or another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. That connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne files a Standard.site publication and document in your own repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates the same record when you publish again. Unpublishing removes the document from your PDS.

PDF (Typst) compiles the manuscript on this device with bundled fonts, equations and diagrams included, and reports any source or asset problem before the export. You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial annotations are stripped from the exported copy; your saved source keeps them.

13 · Your work

Folios, export & publishing

One piece per folio. Salt Roads, its outline and a scratch file of cut paragraphs share a collection and nothing else.

Folios are separate documents with separate dossiers. Switch between them from the drawer. Each keeps its own word count, last-updated time and, if you want, its own layout settings.

Export a folio as Markdown, standalone HTML, plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup: a JSON file with the brief, the folios and their content. All of it is under File in the masthead.

Share publishes a public reading view of a folio. Anyone with the link can read it and nobody can edit it. Unpublish takes it down at once.

Publish to your PDS by connecting Bluesky or another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. That connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne files a Standard.site publication and document in your own repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates the same record when you publish again. Unpublishing removes the document from your PDS.

PDF (Typst) compiles the manuscript on this device with bundled fonts, equations and diagrams included, and reports any source or asset problem before the export. You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial annotations are stripped from the exported copy; your saved source keeps them.

an account. See [the House and fluid desk guide](docs/flow-and-context.md) for
context inheritance, margin behavior and sync boundaries.

## The editorial room

The manuscript’s margins hold comments, editor notes, sources and connections.
Click a passage marker to unfold its conversation beside the draft. The **Cast**,
**Rubric**, **Marginalia** and **Apparatus** panels remain available for browsing;
their tabs show unread work. Automatic focus quiets the surrounding room during
sustained writing, with a manual override in the review controls.

### The room reads as you write

Convening the room is deliberate and expensive — five model calls over the
whole manuscript. Alongside it, a background pass runs on a narrower brief:
once you've written **~300 net new words** _and_ stopped typing for **two
minutes**, all five editors read **only the new paragraphs**, plus a digest of
how the draft has been moving.

Those arrive as quieter "in passing" notes in the Cast panel. Two spend guards
sit on top — a five-minute floor between passes and a per-session cap — because
this runs without you asking. Turn it off with **Read as I write** in the room
settings.

The same digest goes along when you _do_ press Convene, so the deliberate pass
knows the trajectory rather than re-reading a cold snapshot.

### The rubric grades against _this_ piece

The default signed-in check first attempts one typed judgement over the enabled
criteria, including custom criteria. **Ask the editors** runs the separate room
reading; Twyne also tries that path when the quick check is unavailable.

In the room reading, the static feature scorer measures shape — sentence-length variance,
type-token ratio, paragraph balance. It never reads the brief, so fluent prose
about the wrong subject used to score 10/10 on three categories.

That path’s **Target Fit** judge scores relevance independently of craft, and caps
every shape-derived criterion by it. Lowering target fit can only ever lower
the grade, never raise it.

The criteria themselves are yours to shape. Twyne ships a fixed spine so a
score in March means the same thing in June; you can disable or reweight any of
it, add criteria of your own ("stays in second person", "every section ends on
an image") for the room to judge, or ask it to **suggest criteria** fitted to
your format — proposals you accept, never applied silently. Customise anything
and a second "by your weights" score appears beside the editorial grade. Every
pass is recorded, so the panel shows the run of grades rather than a snapshot.

## Voice

| What                                       | Needs                                             |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Hear an editor, memo, or review read aloud | BYOK speech provider, or ElevenLabs v4 through your Not Organic wallet |
| Read the selection (or whole draft) aloud  | same                                              |
| Record a spoken margin note                | microphone + BYOK or hosted **transcription**     |
| Answer the interview out loud              | same                                              |

Each of the five editors has their own voice, per provider — Fish Audio names
voices by id and OpenAI by name, so the mapping is per-provider rather than one
shared field. Spoken notes keep **both** the recording and the transcript: the

On a narrow screen the slip starts as a compact receipt; open it to see the
details or file it to clear the corner. A relevant margin card takes priority
over the receipt, and opening a conversation clears ambient dock furniture.
The ink ribbon stays beside the word count as the manuscript scrolls. Its
reading has a text alternative and does not announce changes while you write.

### A way in, and the pneumatic post

While stuck, Jev's unresolved-passage Noul must reach 0.6 before a single **A way
in** item is offered. In the same budgeted request, a Choice selects a short prompt
from fixed options: say it plainly, start with a concrete detail, return to the
audience and purpose, pick up an earlier thread, or leave TK and move on. Code
supplies the wording from templates and the dossier; System One selects rather
than writes prose. The earlier-thread option needs an actual matched echo, and
the card links the best available echo for its passage.

With no client, a local stuck reading can supply the plain-sentence prompt only
after strong churn (at least 0.6) and the writer's learned stuck pause. A configured
client's budget skip or failed judgement does not count as confirmation. Late
answers cannot offer help after the passage or mode changes. Only one way-in item
is live at once; dismissing it keeps it dismissed for that passage during the
mounted conductor session. It leads while stuck and waits, with an explicit
policy reason, in every other reading or at another passage.

`FlowSnapshot.heldKinds` is the pneumatic post's tally: held items by kind, beside

python3 - <<'EOF'
p='README.md'
s=open(p).read()
old=s[s.index("### The room reads as you write"):s.index("### The rubric grades against _this_ piece")]
new='''### The room reads as you write

Twyne acts without being asked. The buttons remain, but as shortcuts rather
than the way work starts.

- **The editors read on their own.** Once **200 words** are new or rewritten
  since their last reading _and_ you have paused for **a minute**, all five
  editors read the changed paragraphs, plus a digest of how the draft has been
  moving. Rewrites count as much as new material. A folio they have never read
  is read on its own once it reaches 500 words. What they last read is kept
  per folio, so reopening a folio that already has notes stays quiet. Spend
  guards: five minutes between passes and eight passes a session. Turn it off
  with **Read as I write** in the room settings.
- **Quotations lead to passages.** Every passage an editor quotes in a note or
  reply links to the sentence it came from. Matching is literal: typography,
  case and spacing are normalised, `…` elisions are followed within one
  paragraph, and the note's own words choose between repeated phrases. A
  quotation that is ambiguous, or no longer in the draft, stays unlinked and
  says why. Links are re-checked whenever the draft changes.
- **Settled notes stay settled.** Mark a note **intentional** or **later** and
  that editor will not raise the same passage again until its text changes.
  The decisions go to the editors as context too.
- **Research needs no setup.** With your own model, it finds the claims that
  need a source. Signed in without one, Twyne picks out figures, quotations,
  appeals to authority and dated events from the text and Jev confirms which
  really need a source. Fiction is read as fiction. A failed pass or claim
  tries again after 30 seconds, 2 minutes and 10 minutes. The panel always
  says why research is idle: waiting for a pause, draft too short, no claims,
  all covered, or finished.

The same digest goes along when you _do_ press **Get notes**, so the deliberate
pass knows the trajectory rather than re-reading a cold snapshot.

'''
s=s.replace(old,new,1)
old='''The default signed-in check first attempts one typed judgement over the enabled
criteria, including custom criteria. **Ask the editors** runs the separate room
reading; Twyne also tries that path when the quick check is unavailable.'''
assert old in s

criteria, including custom criteria. The editors then read each new version on
their own, at most once every ten minutes, in the background so the grade stays
on screen. Their notes survive later quick checks and say when they are about
an earlier version. **Ask them now** reads the current version straight away;
Twyne also takes the room path when the quick check is unavailable.''',1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

content.content:
## Interaction contract

- Hovering or focusing a passage marker reveals its associated margin card and
  connections. Clicking a comment or persona note unfolds its full conversation
  in that margin slot. Suggestions use the same placement service.
- One conversation owns the foreground at a time. Switching preserves separate
  unsent reply drafts for the mounted editor session; reloading does not preserve
  those unsent drafts. Sent replies retain the existing storage behavior.
- On narrow screens or with automatic margin reading disabled, the existing
  anchored card provides the fallback. Ambient dock cards yield to open threads,
  tools and selection actions. Open margin cards adapt to viewport changes.
- Cards follow document scrolling and step around tools and expanded threads.
  Escape closes the active conversation. Selection actions yield while a thread
  or suggestion is open.
- Fallback comment, persona-note and suggestion cards follow their passage too.
  A passive listener on the manuscript scroller and resize/reflow updates share
  one animation frame. Cards without a margin slot tuck below or above the live
  passage; slot conversations keep the existing margin handshake. A passage fully
  outside the visible manuscript closes a fallback card without a pin or draft.
  Pinned notes and unsent drafts stay clamped on screen. Split marks count as
  visible while any fragment remains in view.
- Manual focus remains available. Automatic focus fades workspace chrome without
  collapsing the writer's side panels. Interacting with controls or a conversation
  prevents automatic focus from hiding them. A manual exit overrides automatic
  focus temporarily.

## Focus and assistance

`flow-state.ts` reads typing cadence; `flow-profile.ts` learns pause thresholds and
item preferences locally. Working shows a small selection, settling holds new
items, flow clears ambient cards, and stuck favors one relevant item plus its
connections. `flow-conductor.ts` combines these signals with budgeted Jev calls.
Local connections are candidates, not claims of semantic certainty. Drift checks
propose amendments rather than silently rewriting the dossier.

| Reading  | What the margin does                          |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Working  | Offers a small selection of relevant items.   |
| Settling | Keeps existing items and holds new arrivals.  |
| Flow     | Clears ambient cards and holds arrivals.      |
| Stuck    | Favors one relevant item and its connections. |

### Galley slips
`FlowSnapshot.heldKinds` is the pneumatic post's tally: held items by kind, beside
the total `held`. It includes only policy-held items, including a waiting way in;
dismissed items do not count. The margin can name what is waiting without showing
the cards during a quiet run.

Cover lookups can be disabled in review controls. Book titles go to Open Library;
record titles go to MusicBrainz and covers come from the Cover Art Archive.
Cadence profiles stay on this device. Diagnostics may contain draft excerpts,
titles, dossier changes and model decisions: inspect an export before sharing it.

## Storage and sync

`house-store.ts` serializes local edits, verifies IndexedDB writes and emits
`twyne:house-changed`. Each edit advances the whole snapshot's timestamp, including
collection membership changes and withdrawals. House state sync runs on both the
House page and the editor, with a live Convex subscription and reconnect refresh.

House, collections and charter use the newer complete snapshot; this is
last-write-wins, not a per-field collaborative merge. Ledger entries are unioned
by ID. A stale server upload may contribute history but cannot replace a newer
snapshot. Local history retains 500 entries; server history is paginated. Signed-out
writing remains local. The current local House is shared within the browser profile,
as with the existing local folio store.

Ledger acknowledgements are tracked per account in IndexedDB, separately from
the server's bounded history window. An acknowledged entry is not uploaded again
just because it is absent from the latest pull. Partial uploads retry only the
unacknowledged batches; persisting an acknowledgement can retry without repeating
the accepted server mutation.

The margin handshake lives in `margin-surface.ts`: a card reserves a slot before
the editor mounts its full conversation, then receives geometry updates. Pending
reservations survive the old card closing. Editor request tokens prevent slower
opens from replacing a more recently selected conversation.

### Source map

| Contract                           | Implementation                                                                                                              |
| ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Context assembly and provenance    | [`house-model.ts`](../src/utils/house-model.ts), [`model-context.ts`](../src/utils/model-context.ts)                        |
| Local persistence and account sync | [`house-store.ts`](../src/utils/house-store.ts), [`house-sync.ts`](../src/utils/house-sync.ts)                              |
| Cadence and learned preferences    | [`flow-state.ts`](../src/utils/flow-state.ts), [`flow-profile.ts`](../src/utils/flow-profile.ts)                            |
| Gathering and surfacing            | [`flow-conductor.ts`](../src/components/editor/extensions/flow-conductor.ts), [`flow-items.ts`](../src/utils/flow-items.ts) |
| Conversation placement             | [`margin-surface.ts`](../src/utils/margin-surface.ts), [`flow-surface.tsx`](../src/components/in-flow/flow-surface.tsx)     |

## Verification

Focused tests cover inheritance, provenance, quiet-mode surfacing, focus overrides,
session qualification and history, teardown/remount, typed way-in selection and
dismissal, held-kind tallies, cadence transitions and learned thresholds, margin
registration, fallback viewport clamping, card collision placement, snapshot
deletion semantics, account isolation and stale uploads. Browser checks exercise
the House cabinet and tabs, comment/note/suggestion switching, separate reply
drafts, Escape, scrolling and mobile resizing.

**Separate integration checks:** a live authenticated two-device sync and a
funded model-generation session. Local browser fixtures and mocked backend tests
do not prove these paths.

# Dossier UX cleanup — change summary

A focused pass on the dossier refinery (`/dossier/refine`) and dossier onboarding (`/dossier/create`) to fix three related UX problems:

1. The mode switch (Form / Conversation) was hidden when the writer switched into conversation — only the form side rendered the toggle, so there was no way back without the overloaded "Cancel / Use form" button the conversation chrome was carrying.
2. Several different "close" / "cancel" / "back" buttons were scattered across the dossier routes (top-bar back link, form "Close", conversation "Cancel", and a "Close" on the drift-report panel). They meant different things and made it hard to know what any given click would do.
3. There was no way to start the dossier over from scratch on the refinery page. The only way to "redo" the brief was to either pick a different mode (which kept the answers) or re-onboard from scratch (which lost the manuscript).

## What changed

### 1. Shared top bar — `src/components/onboarding/dossier-top-bar.tsx` (new)

A single component that owns the page-level chrome for both dossier routes:

- **Back link** (left): "← Back to desk" on `/dossier/refine`, "← Back home" on `/dossier/create` (when no folio exists yet).
- **Start over** (refine only): destructive, opens a confirm dialog rather than acting directly.
- **Mode switch** (right): right-aligned Form / Conversation pills, same shape in both directions, persistent across both modes so the writer can always switch back.

### 2. Plumbed existing-brief carry-over through the conversation

`Start over` writes the current folio draft into `localStorage` under a one-shot `twyne-starting-material` slot and routes to `/dossier/create/`. The create route reads it on hydration, then clears it. Both authoring surfaces (form and conversation) now consume it:

- **Form** (`AntiTabulaRasa`): new `initialMaterial` prop seeds the form's existing-material field.
- **Conversation** (`ConversationalInterview`): new `initialMaterial` prop is plumbed into the interview-turn request as `startingMaterial` and forwarded to both the Convex `runInterviewTurn` action and the client-side `runClientInterviewTurn` wrapper. The interview system prompt receives a `--- BEGIN MANUSCRIPT ---` block when present, so the AI orients its first question around the writer's draft rather than rediscovering it from scratch.

### 3. Removed in-body exit buttons

- `AntiTabulaRasa`: dropped its in-body `Close` button and the `onCancel$` prop (the top bar is now the only exit).
- `ConversationalInterview`: dropped its in-body `Cancel` button, the `cancelLabel` prop, and the `cancelOrUseForm` helper that overloaded the Cancel button to mean either "switch to form" or "leave the page". The conversation's `onCancel$` and `onUseForm$` props are kept because the ApplicationNotice recovery flow still uses them and the create route still passes `onUseForm$` for the mode-switch handler.
- Refine route: dropped `onCancel$` from both authoring surfaces; it now leaves via the top bar.

## Files touched

- **New**: `src/components/onboarding/dossier-top-bar.tsx`
- **`src/utils/anti-tabula-rasa.ts`** — added `STARTING_MATERIAL_KEY` constant and `loadStartingMaterial` / `saveStartingMaterial` / `clearStartingMaterial` helpers (lines 14–19, 135–157).
- **`src/components/onboarding/anti-tabula-rasa.tsx`** — new `initialMaterial` prop on `AntiTabulaRasaProps` (line 155); wired into the store's `existingMaterial` (line 207); dropped `onCancel$` prop and the in-body `Close` button (lines 527–535 removed, 169–172 updated).
- **`src/components/onboarding/conversational-interview.tsx`** — new `initialMaterial` prop (line 91); dropped `cancelLabel` (line 99 removed) and `cancelOrUseForm` helper (lines 448–462 removed); `startingMaterial` plumbed into both call sites (lines 287–293 and 333–335).
- **`src/utils/ai-client.ts`** — `InterviewTurnRequest.startingMaterial` added (line 2270); `runClientInterviewTurn` injects the manuscript into the system prompt (lines 2388–2402).
- **`convex/agents.ts`** — `runInterviewTurn` action gained an optional `startingMaterial` arg (lines 727–732); passed into `interviewSystemPrompt` (line 760); system prompt now appends a `--- BEGIN MANUSCRIPT ---` block when present (lines 605–607).
- **`src/routes/dossier/refine/index.tsx`** — replaced the inline top-bar div with `<DossierTopBar>` (lines 269–296 replaced); removed `onCancel$` from `AntiTabulaRasa` and `ConversationalInterview` (lines 411, 419); added `confirmStartOver` handler (lines 188–221) and a `<ThemedDialog>` for the destructive confirm (lines 425–440).

the product direction that followed it: **Twyne acts without being asked.**
Reviews, research and editors' readings run on their own; buttons remain as
shortcuts and overrides, not as the way work starts.

Not yet released. Fold into `CHANGELOG.md` at the next version.

## Principle

A feature that waits for a click before doing its core job is a defect. Each
automatic path has a trigger (folio open, draft change, idle pause, a fresh
quick grade) and spend guards (rate floors, session caps, dedupe by draft
fingerprint). Empty states say what Twyne is about to do, not what to press.
Hosted writers without their own model get the automatic path too.

## 1. Review and research arrive on their own

### Background room — `src/utils/background-room.ts`

| Before                                                         | After                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Existing prose counted as read on every open, so an unread draft was never read until Get notes | What the room last read is stored per folio (`background-room-read:<folioId>`). A folio with no record and no notes starts empty and is read on its own; one with notes from before the record existed counts as read |
| Triggered by 500 **net** new words and a 2-minute pause         | Triggered by 200 words in new or rewritten paragraphs (`diffParagraphs(...).added`) and a 1-minute pause |
| `startBackgroundRoom` had no current draft                      | `currentText` arms the watcher straight away when the draft holds unread work               |

Guards unchanged: `MIN_INTERVAL_MS` (5 min), `MAX_PASSES_PER_SESSION` (8),
`MIN_EDITOR_WORDS` (500) before any reading. `src/routes/editor/index.tsx`
loads the stored baseline and existing notes when the folio opens.

### Rubric — `src/components/rubric/rubric-panel.tsx`

- `autoReadRoom` starts the editors' reading when a live-review quick grade
  arrives for a draft fingerprint the editors have not read, at most every
  `ROOM_READ_FLOOR_MS` (10 min, stored per folio), and only when a hosted
  client or BYOK provider exists.
- `runAnalysis(frontierOnly, quiet)` — a quiet run uses `isReviewing`, so the
  current grade stays on screen instead of the full-panel loader.
- The editors' notes survive later quick checks (`judges` carried forward);
  `judgesFingerprint` marks notes about an earlier version. A reading whose
  draft changed mid-run keeps its notes rather than discarding them.
- Automatic readings snapshot as `automatic` (5-minute spacing) so they cannot
  crowd manual checkpoints out of the 50-entry history; requested readings
  still force a `rubric` checkpoint.
- The Editors tab says `soon` / `reading…` instead of `0`.

### Research — `src/utils/background-research.ts`, `src/utils/research-candidates.ts` (new)

- Hosted writers without their own model: `claimCandidates` finds figures,
  attributed quotations, appeals to authority and dated events by rule;
  one batched Jev request (`candidateRequest`) confirms which need a source
  (Noul ≥ 0.6), with fiction instructed to ignore invented events.
- `ResearchIdleReason` (`waiting`, `too-short`, `no-provider`, `no-claims`,
  `covered`, `pass-done`) replaces the bare "Watching draft".
- Failed passes and failed claims retry on their own at 30 s, 2 min and
  10 min (`scheduleRetry`), then stop and leave the retry control.
- Each Deep trace row says what found / no match / failed means and offers
  Go to the claim.

## 2. Passage grounding and card meaning

- **Quotations** — `src/utils/quote-grounding.ts` (new). `extractQuotations`
  reads paired quotation marks and Markdown block quotes; `resolveQuotation`
  normalises typography, case and whitespace, follows `…` elisions within one
  paragraph, never crosses paragraphs, and breaks ties with the note's
  surrounding words (same paragraph only, stopwords removed). Ties stay
  `ambiguous`; missing text stays `unmatched`. `renderGroundedMarkdown` wraps
  resolved quotations as links after safe Markdown rendering. Links are
  re-resolved on `twyne:content` and again in the editor on click
  (`twyne:reveal-quote`, `findQuotationRange`). Used by the Cast panel notes
  and replies and the in-manuscript note card.
- **Relationship cards** — `flow-conductor.ts` asks a Choice alongside the echo
  Noul (`ECHO_RELATIONS`); shared vocabulary only suppresses the card. The card
  shows both passages and offers That's the connection / Not how I read it.
- **Settled notes** — `src/utils/note-decisions.ts` (new). Intentional / later
  per note, stored on this device (`note-decisions:<folioId>`). A decision
  stands while its anchor still resolves in the draft; `withoutSettled` drops
  repeat notes from the same editor in explicit and background passes, and
  `decisionsDigest` goes to the editors as context.

## 3. Versions — `src/utils/revision-history.ts`, `version-history-panel.tsx`

- `describeRevision` writes one sentence per comparison from the changes
  (rewrote / cut / added, and whose notes the rewrites reached).
- Changes are labelled Rewritten / Cut / New passage with Before and After.
- `notesTouchedBy` shows editor notes whose anchor was in the old passage and
  is gone from the new one — evidence the change reached the note, not proof
  it answered it.
- Optional intent on Save checkpoint (`RevisionSnapshot.intent`) names the
  checkpoint. Counts move under Size of the change.

## Answers to the brief's open questions

- **Cast cards / "further on as you read".** Cast cards are `PersonasPanel`
  notes (`personas-panel.tsx`); the "Further on in this piece" card is an
  `echo` flow item from `flow-conductor.ts`, rendered by `flow-surface.tsx`.
- **Editor review and the manual click.** The quick check never runs the
  editors; the click started their reading. It now starts on its own.
- **"Watching graph".** Research went idle silently when there was no
  provider, the draft was short, no claims were found or all were covered.
  Each is now a named state, and hosted writers have a provider path.
- **Jev's decisions.** Jev confirms echo relevance and relationship, hosted
  research claims, note quality gates, and the quick grade; the relationship
  label and the research claim rows surface those decisions.
- **Revision information.** Snapshots hold full HTML and Typst source, so
  passage-level before/after is exact; intent is now recorded when given, and
  note evidence is derived from stored editor notes.

## Not covered

- Unread markers for finished reviews.
- Rejected relationship readings are dismissed, not recorded as a rejected
  reading.
- Note decisions do not sync between devices.
- Manual screenshots for the Cast notes, echo card, Apparatus Deep trace and
  Version history predate these changes.

## Tests

`quote-grounding.test.ts`, `note-decisions.test.ts`,
`research-candidates.test.ts`, additions to `background-room.test.ts` and
`revision-history.test.ts`; `personas-markdown-wiring.test.ts` updated for the
grounded renderer.

I've updated the docs to describe the autonomous behaviour. Typecheck and lint pass, and no tests pin this text; nothing is committed.

**The manual (`src/routes/docs/`)**, in the Morgan / Salt Roads voice:

/**
 * Supertonic — the browser's own voice.
 *
 * Supertonic is a full neural TTS model that runs on-device through
 * transformers.js (WebGPU when available, WASM otherwise). It is the
 * free/offline voice: no API key, no server, no account — the writer
 * downloads the voice pack once and the reading costs nothing after that.
 *
 * Download-and-evict lives in `models-cache.ts`. This module is the thin
 * layer that:
 *
 *   - detects whether the browser can run the model at all,
 *   - reports bundle state (not-downloaded / downloading / ready),
 *   - redirects transformers.js fetches to the downloaded bytes via
 *     `env.fetch`, so synthesis works with no network access,
 *   - turns a passage into a WAV clip, chunked at sentence boundaries.
 *
 * It is only imported by the Supertonic branch of `runClientVoiceSpeech`, so
 * the transformers.js runtime stays out of the main bundle.
 */

} from "./browser-inference";

I'm planning which manual chapters need narration scripts, likely covering all sections except the launch-film itself, while deciding how to handle the shortcuts table since it doesn't narrate naturally and might need a shortened version.

For the narration voice, I'm thinking of framing each chapter as a third-person story about Morgan Vale working on a draft called Salt Roads, told in the existing narrator voice (Gacrux), with each chapter around 150-250 words so the total stays manageable. For generation, I'm leaning toward breaking each chapter into paragraph segments, generating TTS per segment, then concatenating them with ffmpeg into one audio file per chapter, stored as m4a or mp3 for broad browser compatibility.

Settling on AAC-encoded m4a at a low mono bitrate (48kbps) for safety across browsers since Opus-in-WebM support on Safari is uncertain — that keeps each chapter file small, roughly 360KB per minute, and the whole set around 9MB. I also want a transcript shown under the player for accessibility, with the narration text and metadata (title, voice, duration, src) living in a shared TS module so the generation script can read from the same source.

For the generator script, I'm planning to use Bun to import that TS module directly, avoiding duplicated text, and reuse the existing falRun helper from the video pipeline's lib.mjs rather than reimplementing the fal queue API call — I should check falRun's signature before wiring it in.

For the UI, I'm picturing a compact ManualNarration component per section with a "Listen · 1:12" button, play/pause, a progress bar, and a transcript disclosure, built on top of a native audio element for simplicity.

I should check how ManualVideo handles the existing capture-level play listener that pauses other media when one starts, since extending that logic to cover audio elements too (not just video) would keep playback consistent. It'd also be nice to support continuous "listen to the whole manual" playback that auto-advances and scrolls to the next chapter when narration ends.

I'll keep this simple: default to auto-continuing into the next chapter's narration, and only auto-scroll into view if the reader appeared to be following along (i.e., the finished player was visible in viewport), respecting reduced-motion settings.

For voice, I'll stick with Gacrux, the existing narrator, keeping a single consistent voice rather than complicating things with multi-speaker support, even though Gemini TTS technically allows it. The story should frame Morgan as the subject in third-person present tense, mirroring the manual's voice but told as narrative rather than instruction — which means I need to go through the manual's actual chapter text to write narration that stays accurate to the real app, so let me pull the prose for each section.
