content.content:
1	=== getting-started
2	01 · At the desk Begin a piece Meet Morgan Vale, who has four thousand words about salt caravans and no idea what the essay is for. This manual follows that draft, Salt Roads, from a brief to a proof. Twyne is a writing desk with an editorial room attached. You write on the page. A small cast of editors reads in the margin, each with a different job, and nothing they say changes a word until you say so. Three habits make the room worth having: Say what the piece is for. The dossier holds the reader, the goal and the shape of the piece. Editors with a brief give better notes than editors guessing. Write first, read notes later. Your draft saves on this device as you type. The editors, the grade and the research read it on their own when you pause; there is nothing to press. The margin holds feedback beside the passage it belongs to, and waits until you look up. Revise on your own terms. Follow a note to its passage, argue with it, ask a different editor, or check the galley proof . Every change is yours to make or refuse. Go to the writing desk →
3	
4	=== dossier
5	02 · At the desk The dossier Morgan's first draft of Salt Roads was beautiful and pointless. The dossier is where you admit what a piece is supposed to do, so the editors can tell you whether it does it. Before the room opens, it asks a short series of questions. They feel like paperwork and they are the opposite: a dossier is the difference between an editor saying "this paragraph is weak" and an editor saying "this paragraph loses the reader you said you were writing for." Answer briefly and honestly. You can change any answer later. Ten sections, and what each is really asking: Working title. A name the room can use. It does not have to be the final one. Form. Essay, memo, chapter, dispatch, proposal. The shape sets expectations about length and manners. Reader. One real person, not a demographic. "A friend who hates travel writing" beats "general readers." Intent. What should be different in the reader when they finish? This is the question Morgan could not answer, and the one that fixed the essay. Voice. How it should feel to read, not just how it should sound. Non-negotiables. Sources to keep, jargon to avoid, the anecdote that must survive every cut. Landing. How you will know the draft has done its job. "The reader can picture the journey" is a test an editor can apply. Particulars. A few follow-up questions drawn from your own answers, to sharpen the softest ones. Prior material and References. Earlier drafts, field notes, links: anything the room should read, with a line on why it matters. The working copy grades each answer as you type, from vague to specific, and counts how many answers are carrying weight. A red mark is not a failure. It is the room telling you which question it would ask first. When the piece changes its mind: choose Refine the dossier at the desk and rewrite the answer that no longer holds. Each filing is kept as an edition, and the room reads the new one on its next pass.
6	
7	=== house
8	03 · At the desk The House & collections Salt Roads is the second of five coastal essays. Morgan is not going to type the same reader into five dossiers. The House is everything you would otherwise repeat: the reader you usually write for, the standards you always hold, the tone of the whole enterprise. A collection narrows that for a series. A folio is one manuscript with its own dossier. Context flows downward, and the most specific layer wins: House Your reusable audience, purpose and standards. Collection Shared context for a series of related pieces. Folio One manuscript, with its own dossier. A filled-in folio field overrides its collection, which overrides the House. Leave a field blank and it inherits. Working titles belong to each folio alone. Charter articles are the exception: they accumulate, so a House rule applies to every piece even when a collection adds rules of its own. Dossier The brief that tells the room what a piece is for. Charter Standards you require or prefer, at House, collection or folio level. "Every claim grounded in a concrete scene" is a Charter article. Edition A saved version of the dossier, with its source and reason. Amendment A proposed change to the dossier, usually offered from the margin. It takes effect only when you file it. Open the House to arrange collections, inspect what a folio inherited, and read the register of changes. "What the models read" is the assembled dossier and charter exactly as the editors receive it; each tool adds its own instructions and excerpts on top. The Engine room holds developer diagnostics and nothing a writer needs. If the editors start asking about something you never told them: look in the register. A collection default or an inherited Charter article is usually the answer, and the source stamp on each field says which.
9	
10	=== flow
11	04 · At the desk Writing in flow Morgan writes in long runs and resents anything that interrupts one. The room is built to wait. While you work, Twyne can bring comments, sources, books, records and echoes of your earlier writing into the margin, each beside the passage it concerns. Nothing pops up over the page. Hover or focus a marker to see what it connects to; select it to open the conversation in the same margin. A quieter page Automatic focus reads your typing cadence. When you have been writing steadily for a while, it quiets the room: new cards wait, controls recede, and the page is the only thing left. Pause, or reach for the room, and it comes back. You can also enter focus yourself with Zen in the manuscript status bar, and leave it with Esc . Help when you need it When a passage stalls, the margin may offer a single connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are offers, not corrections; ignore them and they go away. If what you are writing drifts from the dossier, the room may propose an amendment. It never rewrites the brief behind your back. Why two passages are side by side Halfway through Salt Roads, Morgan writes about the salt merchant's ledger, and a card appears: Earlier in this piece. Unpaid promise. The opening said the ledger would explain the road, and nothing has explained it yet. The card names the relationship (an unpaid promise, a tension, an echo, a repetition, or the same subject) and says in a sentence why it matters. It shows both passages; select either to go to it. A relationship is a reading, not a fault. Some promises are meant to stay open. Choose That's the connection if the reading is right, or Not how I read it to set the card aside for good. A card matched only on shared words says so, rather than pretending to know more. Your controls: Automatic review, margin tools, automatic focus and cover lookups each have their own switch in the review controls. The desk learns your timing and preferences on this device. Cover lookups are the one feature here that talks to the outside world: they send book or record titles to external catalogues.
12	
13	=== the-piece
14	05 · At the desk The piece Some problems only show up across the whole draft: the voice that shifts, the name spelled two ways, the character who vanishes for a chapter. Useful without a model The piece runs on this device, with no model and no cost. It watches first-person stance, similar names, and the conventions your draft mostly follows: spelling, small numbers, quotation marks, dashes and list punctuation. It also maps where each recurring name appears across the headed sections. A finding is a pattern worth a look. Whether it is a problem is your call. Choose Stance, Names, Style or Presence to see that lens on the page. Open a finding for its passages and the actions it offers. On a narrow screen the desk sits below the writing area, and Close gives the space back to the draft. Zen hides it while you write. Know what the score means The ≈ sign marks an estimate. Consistency can move as you revise, because local rules re-count; that movement is not a new editorial opinion. Score details separates the measures made by rule from those made by review. An overall estimate appears at about 150 words. Confirm with a full read asks for a fresh editorial reading of the current draft. It needs automatic review switched on, at least 500 words, and a signed-in model service. The desk says so when a request cannot run. Edit again afterwards and the score becomes an estimate until the new draft has been read. Your choices stay yours. Fixes change only the listed passages, and Undo reverses them. A deliberate exception stays with the folio on this device. Above 80,000 characters the desk pauses these checks and asks you to divide the work into folios.
15	
16	=== writing-instruments
17	06 · At the desk Writing instruments A sentence that is almost right. A paragraph that sounds like one you wrote earlier. A scene with no sound in it. Each gets a tool that opens beside the words, not instead of them. Select text in the manuscript and the tools that fit it appear. A single word offers Alternatives. A passage offers Rework, with Hear it read, Threads, Scene bench and Task desk under More. The Compositor also opens Task desk from Review. Close a tool, or press Escape, and the page is back. Work on a whole sentence Morgan's opening line has been rewritten nine times. Sentence bench keeps the working wording at the top with Use this wording beside it. Rewrite lists complete earlier wordings, rule-based changes and model alternatives, each with its word-count change. Choose one to make it the working wording, or Compare to keep the original alongside. Hover or keyboard-focus a candidate to preview it in place on the page. How these were checked shows the grammar status and any meaning the check could not verify. Undo restores the edit. Words offers bundled thesaurus choices shown inside the full sentence, and underlines words you have already used in the paragraph. A synonym can change the meaning, so read the sentence again. With the Words in context pack installed, On-device alternatives adds local word predictions. Likely is not the same as right. Place shows where else the sentence could sit, with the sentences on either side. Read each arrangement before choosing Move here; the reasons come from local rules and no model has judged them. Hear reads the sentence before, the working wording and the sentence after through your narration player, using a downloaded local voice or your voice service. Follow a thread Threads pairs exact sentences from the manuscript that may be talking to each other. Hover or keyboard-focus a pair to mark both passages; choose a sentence to go to it. Local checks find repeated wording, shared vocabulary and possible references. A relation stays unverified until the judgement service has read it; a model reading names its source and shows how sure it is. For an exact repeat, you can remove either occurrence as one undoable edit. Repetition is sometimes the point, so leaving both is always an option. If the passage changes, reopen the instrument before trusting its earlier reading. Follow an entity through the piece In the instrument desk, choose Entities. Select a name candidate to see every mention across the sections and read the source passages. The index is local and literal: it can include places or ordinary capitalised words, and a candidate is not a confirmed character. Spelling variants are grouped by a local rule. Choose a reading, then Read with judgement model to inspect relationships by section, compare a named attribute such as the colour of a coat, or try blind dialogue attribution. The blind reading hides speaker tags and is allowed to answer Unknown. Every result keeps its exact evidence and full distribution. A possible contradiction is a lead to chase, and a model's confidence is not a grade for your characterisation. Read paragraphs; keep your choices Open Paragraph readings in The piece to see each paragraph's scores and narrating tense. Local English cues and Jev readings are labelled separately so you know which is which. Inspect distributions and context shows the exact paragraph behind a reading, including a split or uncertain result. These readings stand apart from the whole-piece grade and its estimate. Keeping a deliberate style or name exception saves the existing uses in the folio's Charter. New drift can still be flagged. Check these again removes the exception. A save notice tells you if the choice could only be kept on this device. Invite an editor into the work Sentence bench, each Threads pair and Scene bench offer Ask the room . Your judgement model, Jev when selected, reads the passage, your working proposal and the tool's question, then chooses the editor most likely to help. It may choose no one. You can also pick an editor yourself. The chosen editor replies in Marginalia, with their portrait and name above the critique. The saved question keeps the original passage separate from any unapplied wording or scene idea, so the editor knows what is on the page and what is only proposed. The reply uses your writing model and your provider settings govern the charge. If the source changes before the request is filed, reopen the instrument. The manuscript stays yours. Leave a question at the Task desk Some questions need more than a margin note: "does the ford scene contradict the field notes?" Choose Writing review or Research selected account resources, confirm the reference passage, and describe what would help. For research, enable resource access in Account sources and choose up to three texts. The task reads those and only those; it does not search the open web. Sign in with Not Organic and sync the folio before queueing. Once your account accepts the request, the work continues on the server after you close the tab, using your hosted model and account credit. Come back to this folio's Task desk for the status, the result, the saved passage and the source excerpts. If the draft has moved on, read the earlier context before acting on the answer. You can cancel unfinished work. A request already with a provider may still finish and incur its charge, but its result is discarded. Mark a returned result Useful or Not useful and add a comment; the feedback is saved with the task. Results are proposals, never edits. Keep a few tools on your device From Task desk, choose On-device tools. Passage connections, Words in context and Say it are separate English-language packs, each with its download size shown. Download & load is an explicit choice, with Stop download and Remove pack beside it. Model files come from Hugging Face and the shared runtime from jsDelivr; keep the page open for the first load. Once installed, these tools use no account credit, and your passages and recordings never leave the device. Passage connections compares nearby passages you choose. Its similarity score is an invitation to read closer; it does not prove a repetition or a missing transition. For Say it , install the speech pack, select a sentence, then record up to a minute or pick an audio clip. Review the transcript before using it as a candidate wording. Browsers can clear or evict storage, so a pack may one day need downloading again. See what a scene gives you Scene bench takes stock of a passage by sense: place, time, light, sound, movement and pressure, each backed by exact quotes from your selection. The local English scan names the cue it found. A cue it did not find may still be there in a form it does not recognise. An optional judgement reading can select evidence and assess pressure; its service and cost appear before you ask for it. Hear the passage uses your narration player. Ideas stay beside the evidence. Under Try a detail, save a sound or an image you want to try without touching the manuscript. Image, sound and motion briefs keep those additions clearly separate from the original passage, ready to paste into another tool. See it as a reader might can sketch a picture of the scene, but scene pictures are off until you enable them in Settings, because generating one spends credit. Above 12,000 characters or 64 sentences the bench asks for a shorter selection.
18	
19	=== room
20	07 · The editorial room Your editors Five resident voices, each reading for something different. No single editor is right about everything, which is rather the point of having five. You will come to know them by their faces. The same portraits accompany each editor's critiques, margin replies and rubric readings, so a glance tells you whether it was the sceptic or the copy chief who objected. A custom editor without a portrait signs with their initials. From any writing instrument, Ask the room brings one of them into the question you are already working on. They read without being asked Morgan never convenes the room. Once a draft reaches 500 words, the editors read it on their own the first time Morgan pauses. After that they come back whenever about 200 words are new or rewritten and the page has been quiet for a minute. A rewrite counts as much as new material, so tightening the harbour section brings fresh notes. They read only the paragraphs that changed, along with a sketch of how the draft has been moving. Those notes arrive marked in passing, lighter than the notes you ask for. There are at least five minutes between readings and a limit per session, because this spends model calls without a click. Get notes is still there when you want the whole room now. Read as I write, in the room settings, turns the automatic reading off. Every quotation leads somewhere When Marguerite quotes three lines of Salt Roads in one note, each quotation is underlined and goes to its own passage, not to the first one. Twyne matches the words literally. It ignores curly quotes, capitals and spacing, and follows a quotation with an ellipsis in it. If the same phrase appears twice, the words around the quotation in the note decide which one is meant. A quotation that could be either, or that is no longer in the draft because Morgan has since rewritten it, gets a dotted underline instead of a link. Hover over it to see why. Twyne would rather leave a quotation unplaced than send you to the wrong sentence, and it checks again every time the draft changes. Meant as written, or for later The abrupt ending of the ferry scene is deliberate, and Mlle. Sceptique will not stop pointing it out. Choose intentional on her note. Choose later for a note you agree with but will deal with after this draft. Either way, that editor will not raise the same passage again until its words change. The settled note steps back on the page, and selecting the label again undoes the decision. Decisions are kept on this device. Arrange your room Custom editors: Visit the Room of Editors to add, edit or reorder the cast. An editor needs a name, a role and a description of how they talk; the more specific the description, the more consistently the model stays in character. Morgan's Route Reader exists because nobody else in the room cared about distances. Changing the model Each editor is only as good as the model reading for them. A careful, precise model makes Mlle. Sceptique sharper. A warmer one makes Sœur Encourageante more generous. In Preferences you can assign different models to different jobs, and the room adapts.
21	
22	=== rubric
23	08 · The editorial room The galley proof Salt Roads got a B. That is not information. The reasons under the grade are. The static features are the part of the proof that never guesses: sentence length distribution, type-token ratio, citation density, paragraph shape. They are computed on this device, cost nothing and call nothing. They give you a cold, honest picture of the draft's mechanics, and nothing at all about whether it is any good. Quick check When the signed-in service is available, the default check makes one typed judgement request against your enabled criteria, custom ones included. You get a grade without separate verdicts from the five editors. If the quick check is unavailable, Twyne falls back to the room reading. The editors' reading The grade arrives on its own. Once the draft has 500 words and you pause, Twyne runs the quick check. The editors then read the new version themselves, at most once every ten minutes, and the grade stays on screen while they work. Until they finish, the Editors tab says soon rather than showing a zero. Choose Ask them now there if you would rather not wait. When the quick check refreshes after an edit, the editors' notes stay, marked as being about an earlier version until they read the new one. Each editor gives a score and a rationale, and the places where they disagree are usually where the revision is. This path combines editorial verdicts with the static features. Its Target Fit check caps the shape scores when a piece misses the audience or purpose in its dossier, because a beautifully built essay for the wrong reader is still the wrong essay. What the letters mean: A range. Publishable or nearly so. Polish. B range. A solid draft with clear, fixable problems. This is where Salt Roads sits. C range. Doing the work, but a real pass is still needed. D to F range. The important next pass is still ahead. Use the rationale, not the letter: read the explanation beside each criterion and hold it against your own purpose. The rubric is one more reading of the draft. You decide which of its complaints deserve a revision.
24	
25	=== marginalia
26	09 · The editorial room Margin conversations Every argument about a passage happens next to the passage. Your notes, the editors' notes, and the replies between them. Select any passage and choose Comment to leave a note in the margin. Notes belong to the folio and travel with it. Each one can hold replies, and Ask an editor invites a particular voice into the thread when you want a second opinion on your own doubt. Select a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve it there. One conversation is in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. A reply you have not sent survives switching threads during the visit, but not a reload, so send it or lose it.
27	
28	=== apparatus
29	10 · The editorial room Research & citations The 1911 survey, the tide table, the book Morgan keeps paraphrasing. The Apparatus notices them and keeps them in order. The Apparatus does three things: finds sources, keeps them, and cites them. As you write it recognises DOIs, URLs, ISBNs and author-year references in the text. You can also search by query; the panel returns a shortlist with title, author, publisher and a snippet. Save what matters to the bibliography and ignore the rest. The bibliography is formatted in the style you choose, MLA, APA or Chicago, and switches instantly when an editor changes their mind. Copy the whole list to the clipboard in one go. Research that runs itself Morgan does not ask for sources. A short while after Morgan stops typing, the Apparatus reads the draft and picks out what a careful reader would want backed up: the figure about the salt trade, the line quoted from the 1911 survey, the year the harbour closed. It searches for each one and files what it finds under the claim that prompted it. With your own model configured, that model picks the claims. Signed in without one, Twyne finds them in the text and Jev confirms which really need a source. In fiction, invented events are left alone. The panel always says what it is doing: reading the draft, searching, or why it is idle. It might be waiting for a pause, the draft might be too short, there might be no claims that need a source, or every claim may already be covered. Each claim in Deep trace explains its result. Found means sources are on file, so check that they support your wording. No match means the search ran and found nothing, so the claim may need softer wording or a source of your own. Failed means the search broke, which is not the same as finding nothing. Twyne tries a failed search again on its own after thirty seconds, two minutes and ten minutes; retry is there if you want it sooner. Go to the claim shows the sentence in the manuscript. The full Apparatus lives at /apparatus . The citation tab in the right panel shows a quick view of what has been detected without leaving the page.
30	
31	=== account-and-live
32	11 · The editorial room Your account & Live A name for the editors to address you by, and a way to talk to one out loud when typing is too slow. Sign in with Not Organic to carry your account, hosted credits and plan across devices. Your name and picture identify you in the room; your email stays in private account settings and appears nowhere else. You can keep writing locally without ever signing in. Talk opens a voice conversation with an editor, from the compositor, from one of their comments, or from the narration player. Live shows captions, lets you mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose edits as you speak. A proposed edit waits for your approval before it touches the manuscript. Switching folios ends the conversation. Captions and microphone audio are not saved. Live needs a Pro plan or available Twyne welcome credit. A conversation reserves up to $0.50; delegated language requests cap at $0.05 each on top. The voice desk shows these limits before you start, which is why it is worth reading.
33	
34	=== manuscript-tools
35	12 · Your work Manuscript & source tools Headings, tables, a footnote, a pull quote set just so. The page is a real page, and when it is not enough there is the source underneath it. Move through the manuscript Type / at the start of a block to open the insert menu. The outline jumps between headings, and dragging a heading's section handle moves that section with everything under it in one undoable edit. Find and Replace understands whole words, case and regular expressions. Tables and images Tables come with a size picker, captions, row and column tools, cell shading, alignment, borders and reusable visual presets. Images can be dropped, pasted or chosen from disk; select one to set its alt text, caption, alignment, width and see its upload status. Online images are stored with the folio. Deliberately offline work keeps an inline copy instead. Source and proof The Typst workspace lets you edit the source directly and read a paginated proof. A source draft recovers on this device after a reload. Apply a valid draft to update the folio; if another device has changed the base in the meantime, resolve that conflict first. An invalid draft is never applied and stays there for you to fix. Shape the page Notes and equations Inline and display equations accept LaTeX and render on this device. Footnotes and endnotes are edited beside their references. The running header and footer live under View, then Layout, and the proof is where you check their placement. Notes and equations survive HTML and Markdown export intact.
36	
37	=== folios
38	13 · Your work Folios, export & publishing One piece per folio. Salt Roads, its outline and a scratch file of cut paragraphs share a collection and nothing else. Folios are separate documents with separate dossiers. Switch between them from the drawer. Each keeps its own word count, last-updated time and, if you want, its own layout settings. Export a folio as Markdown, standalone HTML, plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup: a JSON file with the brief, the folios and their content. All of it is under File in the masthead. Share publishes a public reading view of a folio. Anyone with the link can read it and nobody can edit it. Unpublish takes it down at once. Publish to your PDS by connecting Bluesky or another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. That connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne files a Standard.site publication and document in your own repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates the same record when you publish again. Unpublishing removes the document from your PDS. PDF (Typst) compiles the manuscript on this device with bundled fonts, equations and diagrams included, and reports any source or asset problem before the export. You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial annotations are stripped from the exported copy; your saved source keeps them. What a revision did Twyne saves checkpoints on its own as you write, and whenever you ask for a grade. Version history describes each comparison in a sentence, written from the changes themselves: Rewrote three passages and cut one. The changes reach passages Marguerite had notes on. Each changed passage is labelled Rewritten, Cut or New passage, with the before and after text together. When a rewrite reaches a passage an editor had a note on, the note is shown beside it. That shows the change reached the passage, not that it answered the note. Save checkpoint takes an optional line saying what the revision was for, such as "pay off the ledger promise", and that line names the checkpoint afterwards. The word and passage counts are still there under Size of the change. Restore always saves the current draft first.
39	
40	=== byok
41	14 · Your work Bring your own key Morgan already pays for a model and would like the editors to use it. Three steps, once. Add a provider. In Preferences , switch on Bring Your Own Key and add an OpenAI, Anthropic or Google key. For anything else, Groq, Together, Rivet, a local server, choose the OpenAI-compatible option and give it the base URL. Test the key. Choose Test key on the provider card. A successful check proves the key reaches the model list, and lets you refresh the models you can pick from. Pick models per feature. The per-feature grid assigns different models to the room, the rubric and the other tools. Spend the expensive model where reading quality matters and leave the rest on something cheaper. Supported providers: OpenAI Anthropic Google OpenAI-compatible (Groq, Together, Rivet, local servers, …) If a connection fails: check the provider and key in Preferences and test again. The desk keeps working while a provider is down; only the editors go quiet.
42	
43	=== privacy
44	15 · Your work Privacy & your data The manuscript is yours. Here is exactly where it goes, and where it does not. API keys are saved in your browser's IndexedDB. A remote BYOK request passes through Twyne's server relay, which forwards your key and the request to the provider you chose and keeps neither. Local model endpoints are called directly. Drafts and folios are saved in your browser profile. Signing out does not erase that local copy. Signing in to an account that has no cloud snapshot can sync the existing local work into it, and signed-in sync is what gives you the same work on another device. AI calls send draft text to whichever model is reading. With your own key, that is the provider you chose, through the relay for remote endpoints. Hosted calls go through Convex and Not Organic, where provider processing and content-logging consent are managed. Published pieces are the only ones anyone else can read. Nothing becomes public until you publish it. Sharing and collaboration grant exactly the access you choose, through their own controls.
45	
46	=== shortcuts
47	16 · Your work Keyboard shortcuts Choose the labels for your keyboard. The same shortcut registry powers this guide and the desk. Shortcut labels (platform.value = "mac")} /> macOS (platform.value = "windows")} /> Windows / Linux
48	
49	=== launch-film
50	The film follows your language choice in Preferences. French readers see the French edition, including narration and on-screen text; English and other languages use the English edition. With Automatic selected, Twyne follows your browser’s language preferences.

=== getting-started
01 · At the desk Begin a piece Meet Morgan Vale, who has four thousand words about salt caravans and no idea what the essay is for. This manual follows that draft, Salt Roads, from a brief to a proof. Twyne is a writing desk with an editorial room attached. You write on the page. A small cast of editors reads in the margin, each with a different job, and nothing they say changes a word until you say so. Three habits make the room worth having: Say what the piece is for. The dossier holds the reader, the goal and the shape of the piece. Editors with a brief give better notes than editors guessing. Write first, read notes later. Your draft saves on this device as you type. The editors, the grade and the research read it on their own when you pause; there is nothing to press. The margin holds feedback beside the passage it belongs to, and waits until you look up. Revise on your own terms. Follow a note to its passage, argue with it, ask a different editor, or check the galley proof . Every change is yours to make or refuse. Go to the writing desk →

=== dossier
02 · At the desk The dossier Morgan's first draft of Salt Roads was beautiful and pointless. The dossier is where you admit what a piece is supposed to do, so the editors can tell you whether it does it. Before the room opens, it asks a short series of questions. They feel like paperwork and they are the opposite: a dossier is the difference between an editor saying "this paragraph is weak" and an editor saying "this paragraph loses the reader you said you were writing for." Answer briefly and honestly. You can change any answer later. Ten sections, and what each is really asking: Working title. A name the room can use. It does not have to be the final one. Form. Essay, memo, chapter, dispatch, proposal. The shape sets expectations about length and manners. Reader. One real person, not a demographic. "A friend who hates travel writing" beats "general readers." Intent. What should be different in the reader when they finish? This is the question Morgan could not answer, and the one that fixed the essay. Voice. How it should feel to read, not just how it should sound. Non-negotiables. Sources to keep, jargon to avoid, the anecdote that must survive every cut. Landing. How you will know the draft has done its job. "The reader can picture the journey" is a test an editor can apply. Particulars. A few follow-up questions drawn from your own answers, to sharpen the softest ones. Prior material and References. Earlier drafts, field notes, links: anything the room should read, with a line on why it matters. The working copy grades each answer as you type, from vague to specific, and counts how many answers are carrying weight. A red mark is not a failure. It is the room telling you which question it would ask first. When the piece changes its mind: choose Refine the dossier at the desk and rewrite the answer that no longer holds. Each filing is kept as an edition, and the room reads the new one on its next pass.

=== house
03 · At the desk The House & collections Salt Roads is the second of five coastal essays. Morgan is not going to type the same reader into five dossiers. The House is everything you would otherwise repeat: the reader you usually write for, the standards you always hold, the tone of the whole enterprise. A collection narrows that for a series. A folio is one manuscript with its own dossier. Context flows downward, and the most specific layer wins: House Your reusable audience, purpose and standards. Collection Shared context for a series of related pieces. Folio One manuscript, with its own dossier. A filled-in folio field overrides its collection, which overrides the House. Leave a field blank and it inherits. Working titles belong to each folio alone. Charter articles are the exception: they accumulate, so a House rule applies to every piece even when a collection adds rules of its own. Dossier The brief that tells the room what a piece is for. Charter Standards you require or prefer, at House, collection or folio level. "Every claim grounded in a concrete scene" is a Charter article. Edition A saved version of the dossier, with its source and reason. Amendment A proposed change to the dossier, usually offered from the margin. It takes effect only when you file it. Open the House to arrange collections, inspect what a folio inherited, and read the register of changes. "What the models read" is the assembled dossier and charter exactly as the editors receive it; each tool adds its own instructions and excerpts on top. The Engine room holds developer diagnostics and nothing a writer needs. If the editors start asking about something you never told them: look in the register. A collection default or an inherited Charter article is usually the answer, and the source stamp on each field says which.

=== flow
04 · At the desk Writing in flow Morgan writes in long runs and resents anything that interrupts one. The room is built to wait. While you work, Twyne can bring comments, sources, books, records and echoes of your earlier writing into the margin, each beside the passage it concerns. Nothing pops up over the page. Hover or focus a marker to see what it connects to; select it to open the conversation in the same margin. A quieter page Automatic focus reads your typing cadence. When you have been writing steadily for a while, it quiets the room: new cards wait, controls recede, and the page is the only thing left. Pause, or reach for the room, and it comes back. You can also enter focus yourself with Zen in the manuscript status bar, and leave it with Esc . Help when you need it When a passage stalls, the margin may offer a single connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are offers, not corrections; ignore them and they go away. If what you are writing drifts from the dossier, the room may propose an amendment. It never rewrites the brief behind your back. Why two passages are side by side Halfway through Salt Roads, Morgan writes about the salt merchant's ledger, and a card appears: Earlier in this piece. Unpaid promise. The opening said the ledger would explain the road, and nothing has explained it yet. The card names the relationship (an unpaid promise, a tension, an echo, a repetition, or the same subject) and says in a sentence why it matters. It shows both passages; select either to go to it. A relationship is a reading, not a fault. Some promises are meant to stay open. Choose That's the connection if the reading is right, or Not how I read it to set the card aside for good. A card matched only on shared words says so, rather than pretending to know more. Your controls: Automatic review, margin tools, automatic focus and cover lookups each have their own switch in the review controls. The desk learns your timing and preferences on this device. Cover lookups are the one feature here that talks to the outside world: they send book or record titles to external catalogues.

=== the-piece
05 · At the desk The piece Some problems only show up across the whole draft: the voice that shifts, the name spelled two ways, the character who vanishes for a chapter. Useful without a model The piece runs on this device, with no model and no cost. It watches first-person stance, similar names, and the conventions your draft mostly follows: spelling, small numbers, quotation marks, dashes and list punctuation. It also maps where each recurring name appears across the headed sections. A finding is a pattern worth a look. Whether it is a problem is your call. Choose Stance, Names, Style or Presence to see that lens on the page. Open a finding for its passages and the actions it offers. On a narrow screen the desk sits below the writing area, and Close gives the space back to the draft. Zen hides it while you write. Know what the score means The ≈ sign marks an estimate. Consistency can move as you revise, because local rules re-count; that movement is not a new editorial opinion. Score details separates the measures made by rule from those made by review. An overall estimate appears at about 150 words. Confirm with a full read asks for a fresh editorial reading of the current draft. It needs automatic review switched on, at least 500 words, and a signed-in model service. The desk says so when a request cannot run. Edit again afterwards and the score becomes an estimate until the new draft has been read. Your choices stay yours. Fixes change only the listed passages, and Undo reverses them. A deliberate exception stays with the folio on this device. Above 80,000 characters the desk pauses these checks and asks you to divide the work into folios.

A passage offers Rework, with Hear it read, Threads, Scene bench and Task desk under More. The Compositor also opens Task desk from Review. Close a tool, or press Escape, and the page is back. Work on a whole sentence Morgan's opening line has been rewritten nine times. Sentence bench keeps the working wording at the top with Use this wording beside it. Rewrite lists complete earlier wordings, rule-based changes and model alternatives, each with its word-count change. Choose one to make it the working wording, or Compare to keep the original alongside. Hover or keyboard-focus a candidate to preview it in place on the page. How these were checked shows the grammar status and any meaning the check could not verify. Undo restores the edit. Words offers bundled thesaurus choices shown inside the full sentence, and underlines words you have already used in the paragraph. A synonym can change the meaning, so read the sentence again. With the Words in context pack installed, On-device alternatives adds local word predictions. Likely is not the same as right. Place shows where else the sentence could sit, with the sentences on either side. Read each arrangement before choosing Move here; the reasons come from local rules and no model has judged them. Hear reads the sentence before, the working wording and the sentence after through your narration player, using a downloaded local voice or your voice service. Follow a thread Threads pairs exact sentences from the manuscript that may be talking to each other. Hover or keyboard-focus a pair to mark both passages; choose a sentence to go to it. Local checks find repeated wording, shared vocabulary and possible references. A relation stays unverified until the judgement service has read it; a model reading names its source and shows how sure it is. For an exact repeat, you can remove either occurrence as one undoable edit. Repetition is sometimes the point, so leaving both is always an option. If the passage changes, reopen the instrument before trusting its earlier reading. Follow an entity through the piece In the instrument desk, choose Entities. Select a name candidate to see every mention across the sections and read the source passages. The index is local and literal: it can include places or ordinary capitalised words, and a candidate is not a confirmed character. Spelling variants are grouped by a local rule. Choose a reading, then Read with judgement model to inspect relationships by section, compare a named attribute such as the colour of a coat, or try blind dialogue attribution. The blind reading hides speaker tags and is allowed to answer Unknown. Every result keeps its exact evidence and full distribution. A possible contradiction is a lead to chase, and a model's confidence is not a grade for your characterisation. Read paragraphs; keep your choices Open Paragraph readings in The piece to see each paragraph's scores and narrating tense. Local English cues and Jev readings are labelled separately so you know which is which. Inspect distributions and context shows the exact paragraph behind a reading, including a split or uncertain result. These readings stand apart from the whole-piece grade and its estimate. Keeping a deliberate style or name exception saves the existing uses in the folio's Charter. New drift can still be flagged. Check these again removes the exception. You can also pick an editor yourself. The chosen editor replies in Marginalia, with their portrait and name above the critique. The saved question keeps the original passage separate from any unapplied wording or scene idea, so the editor knows what is on the page and what is only proposed. The reply uses your writing model and your provider settings govern the charge. If the source changes before the request is filed, reopen the instrument. The manuscript stays yours. Leave a question at the Task desk Some questions need more than a margin note: "does the ford scene contradict the field notes?" Choose Writing review or Research selected account resources, confirm the reference passage, and describe what would help. For research, enable resource access in Account sources and choose up to three texts. The task reads those and only those; it does not search the open web. Sign in with Not Organic and sync the folio before queueing. Once your account accepts the request, the work continues on the server after you close the tab, using your hosted model and account credit. Come back to this folio's Task desk for the status, the result, the saved passage and the source excerpts. If the draft has moved on, read the earlier context before acting on the answer. You can cancel unfinished work. A request already with a provider may still finish and incur its charge, but its result is discarded. Mark a returned result Useful or Not useful and add a comment; the feedback is saved with the task. Results are proposals, never edits. Keep a few tools on your device From Task desk, choose On-device tools. Passage connections, Words in context and Say it are separate English-language packs, each with its download size shown. Download & load is an explicit choice, with Stop download and Remove pack beside it. Model files come from Hugging Face and the shared runtime from jsDelivr; keep the page open for the first load. Once installed, these tools use no account credit, and your passages and recordings never leave the device. Passage connections compares nearby passages you choose. Its similarity score is an invitation to read closer; it does not prove a repetition or a missing transition. For Say it , install the speech pack, select a sentence, then record up to a minute or pick an audio clip. Review the transcript before using it as a candidate wording. Browsers can clear or evict storage, so a pack may one day need downloading again. See what a scene gives you Scene bench takes stock of a passage by sense: place, time, light, sound, movement and pressure, each backed by exact quotes from your selection. The local English scan names the cue it found. A cue it did not find may still be there in a form it does not recognise. An optional judgement reading can select evidence and assess pressure; its service and cost appear before you ask for it. Hear the passage uses your narration player. Ideas stay beside the evidence. Under Try a detail, save a sound or an image you want to try without touching the manuscript. Image, sound and motion briefs keep those additions clearly separate from the original passage, ready to paste into another tool. See it as a reader might can sketch a picture of the scene, but scene pictures are off until you enable them in Settings, because generating one spends credit. Above 12,000 characters or 64 sentences the bench asks for a shorter selection.

=== room
07 · The editorial room Your editors Five resident voices, each reading for something different. No single editor is right about everything, which is rather the point of having five. You will come to know them by their faces. Twyne matches the words literally. It ignores curly quotes, capitals and spacing, and follows a quotation with an ellipsis in it. A quotation that could be either, or that is no longer in the draft because Morgan has since rewritten it, gets a dotted underline instead of a link. Hover over it to see why. Twyne would rather leave a quotation unplaced than send you to the wrong sentence, and it checks again every time the draft changes. Choose later for a note you agree with but will deal with after this draft. Either way, that editor will not raise the same passage again until its words change. The settled note steps back on the page, and selecting the label again undoes the decision. Decisions are kept on this device. Arrange your room Custom editors: Visit the Room of Editors to add, edit or reorder the cast. An editor needs a name, a role and a description of how they talk; the more specific the description, the more consistently the model stays in character. Morgan's Route Reader exists because nobody else in the room cared about distances. Changing the model Each editor is only as good as the model reading for them. A careful, precise model makes Mlle. Sceptique sharper. A warmer one makes Sœur Encourageante more generous. In Preferences you can assign different models to different jobs, and the room adapts.

=== rubric
08 · The editorial room The galley proof Salt Roads got a B. That is not information. The reasons under the grade are. The static features are the part of the proof that never guesses: sentence length distribution, type-token ratio, citation density, paragraph shape. They are computed on this device, cost nothing and call nothing. They give you a cold, honest picture of the draft's mechanics, and nothing at all about whether it is any good. Each editor gives a score and a rationale, and the places where they disagree are usually where the revision is. This path combines editorial verdicts with the static features. Its Target Fit check caps the shape scores when a piece misses the audience or purpose in its dossier, because a beautifully built essay for the wrong reader is still the wrong essay. What the letters mean: A range. Publishable or nearly so. Polish. B range. A solid draft with clear, fixable problems. This is where Salt Roads sits. C range. Doing the work, but a real pass is still needed. D to F range. The important next pass is still ahead. Use the rationale, not the letter: read the explanation beside each criterion and hold it against your own purpose. The rubric is one more reading of the draft. Select any passage and choose Comment to leave a note in the margin. Notes belong to the folio and travel with it. Each one can hold replies, and Ask an editor invites a particular voice into the thread when you want a second opinion on your own doubt. Select a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve it there. One conversation is in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. === apparatus

15 · Your work Privacy & your data The manuscript is yours. Here is exactly where it goes, and where it does not. API keys are saved in your browser's IndexedDB. A remote BYOK request passes through Twyne's server relay, which forwards your key and the request to the provider you chose and keeps neither. Local model endpoints are called directly. -    "A warm, literate audiobook narrator telling a short story about a writer named Morgan. Unhurried and intimate, lightly wry, with clear diction. Let the short sentences land.",

-      "Morgan Vale has four thousand words about salt caravans, and no idea what the essay is for. The draft is called Salt Roads. It has camels in it, and a merchant's ledger, and a harbour that closed, and it does not yet know why any of them are there. This is the story of how it finds out.",

-      "Twyne is a writing desk with an editorial room attached. Morgan writes on the page. Five editors read in the margin, each looking for something different, and not one of them can change a word until Morgan says so.",

-      "Three habits make the room worth having. Say what the piece is for, because editors with a brief give better notes than editors guessing. Write first, and read the notes later: the draft saves as Morgan types, and the editors, the grade and the research all read it on their own whenever Morgan pauses. There is nothing to press. And revise on your own terms. Every note can be followed, argued with, or refused.",
-      "Morgan's first draft of Salt Roads was beautiful and pointless. So before the room opens, it asks a few questions. They feel like paperwork. They are the opposite.",

-      "There is a working title, and a form: an essay, this time. There is the reader, who has to be one real person rather than a demographic, so Morgan writes, a friend who hates travel writing. Then comes the hard one. The intent. What should be different in that friend when they finish? Morgan looks at the question for a long time. The answer, when it comes, fixes the essay.",

-      "The rest go faster. The voice it should have. The non-negotiables, like the story of the salt merchant, which must survive every cut. The landing, a test an editor can actually apply: the reader can picture the journey. And the field notes, with a line on why they matter.",

-      "As Morgan types, each answer is marked from vague to specific. A red mark is not a failure. It is the question the room would ask first. And when the piece changes its mind halfway through, Morgan refines the dossier, and the editors read the new edition on their next pass.",
-      "Salt Roads is the second of five coastal essays, and Morgan is not going to type the same reader into five dossiers. That is what the House is for.",

-      "The House holds what Morgan would otherwise repeat: the usual reader, the standards that always apply, the tone of the whole enterprise. A collection narrows that for the series. And each folio, each single manuscript, keeps its own dossier. Context flows downward, and the most specific layer wins. A field Morgan fills in for Salt Roads overrides the collection, which overrides the House. Leave it blank, and it inherits.",

-      "Standards are the exception. Charter articles add up, so a House rule like, every claim grounded in a concrete scene, applies to every essay, even when the collection adds rules of its own. And when the margin proposes a change to the brief, that amendment waits until Morgan files it.",

-      "One afternoon an editor asks about a reader Morgan never mentioned in Salt Roads. Morgan opens the House and reads the register. It is a collection default, and the stamp on the field says so.",
-      "Morgan writes in long runs, and resents anything that interrupts one. The room is built to wait.",

-      "While Morgan works, the margin fills quietly: a comment, a source, a book cover, an echo of something Morgan wrote last year, each beside the passage it concerns. Nothing pops up over the page. When the typing settles into a steady rhythm, the room goes quiet. New cards wait, the controls recede, and the page is the only thing left. When Morgan pauses, the room comes back.",

-      "Halfway through, Morgan writes about the merchant's ledger, and a card appears beside it. Earlier in this piece. Unpaid promise. The opening said the ledger would explain the road, and nothing has explained it yet. The card shows both passages, and Morgan can go to either one.",

-      "A relationship like that is a reading, not a fault. Some promises are meant to stay open. Morgan chooses, That's the connection, and makes a note to pay it off. When a card is wrong, Not how I read it sets it aside for good. And when a sentence stalls, the margin may offer one short way into the next. Ignore it, and it goes away.",

-      "Some problems only show up across the whole draft. For eleven pages the narrator of Salt Roads says I, and then, without warning, we. And the guide's name is spelled one way in the first section and another way in the second.",

-      "The piece catches both, and it does it on Morgan's own device, with no model and no cost. It watches the first person, similar names, and the conventions the draft mostly follows: spelling, small numbers, quotation marks, dashes. It maps where each recurring name appears, section by section. Morgan chooses Stance, and the turn to we lights up on the page.",

-      "A finding is a pattern worth a look. Whether it is a problem is Morgan's call. The we, it turns out, is deliberate: the caravan has joined up. Morgan keeps it as an exception, and it stays kept. The guide's name is a typo, and Morgan fixes it.",

-      "The score beside the piece wears a small approximately sign, because it is an estimate. When Morgan wants a fresh editorial reading of the whole draft, Confirm with a full read asks for one.",
-      "Morgan's opening line has been rewritten nine times. Morgan selects it, and the tools that fit a whole sentence open beside it, not on top of it.",

-      "Sentence bench keeps the working wording at the top. Below it are Morgan's own earlier versions, rule-based changes, and alternatives from a model, each showing what it adds or cuts. Resting on one previews it in place, between its real neighbours. Morgan reads the fourth twice, and keeps it. Undo is always there.",

-      "Threads pairs sentences that may be talking to each other. One of Morgan's sentences appears twice, word for word, three pages apart. Repetition is sometimes the point. This time it is not, and Morgan removes one copy in a single edit.",

-      "The river crossing feels thin. Scene bench takes stock of it by sense: place, time, light, sound, movement and pressure, each backed by an exact quote. Sound is doing the least work. Morgan saves an idea, the creak of loaded saddlebags, without touching the manuscript.",
-      "And from any of these tools, Ask the room brings the right editor into the question Morgan is already working on. The reply arrives in the margin. The manuscript stays Morgan's.",

-      "Five resident editors read Salt Roads, each for something different. Mademoiselle Sceptique, the devil's advocate. Sœur Encourageante, patron of strengths. Professeur Athenaeum, the scholar. Monsieur Le Stylo, the copy chief. And Le Lecteur, the reader the piece is for. No single editor is right about everything, which is rather the point of having five.",

-      "Morgan never convenes them. Once the draft passed five hundred words, they read it on their own the first time Morgan paused. Now they come back whenever about two hundred words are new or rewritten and the page has been quiet for a minute. Tightening the harbour section counts as much as writing a new one. Their notes arrive marked, in passing.",

-      "When Professeur Athenaeum quotes three lines in one note, each quotation is underlined and leads to its own passage. If a phrase appears twice, the words around it in the note decide which one is meant. If it could be either, or Morgan has since rewritten it, the quotation is left unlinked, with a dotted line that says why. Twyne would rather not guess.",

-      "The ferry scene ends abruptly, on purpose, and Mademoiselle Sceptique will not stop saying so. Morgan marks her note, intentional. A note about the opening's length, Morgan marks for later. Either way, that editor will not raise the same passage again until its words change.",
-      "The grade on Salt Roads is a B. That is not information. The reasons under the grade are.",

-      "Morgan never asked for the grade. Once the draft had five hundred words and Morgan paused, Twyne ran a quick check against the essay's criteria and set the grade on the proof. Then, without being asked, the editors read the new version themselves. The grade stayed on screen while they worked.",

-      "Under it, the static features measure the mechanics: sentence lengths, vocabulary, the shape of the paragraphs. They are cold and honest, and they say nothing about whether the essay is any good. The editors do. Each gives a score and a reason, and where they disagree is usually where the revision is. Target Fit holds the whole thing to the dossier, because a beautiful essay for the wrong reader is still the wrong essay.",

-      "When Morgan edits again, the quick grade refreshes, and the editors' notes stay, marked as being about the earlier version until they have read the new one. Morgan reads the reasons, not the letter, and decides which complaints deserve a revision.",
-      "Every argument about a passage happens next to the passage.",

-      "Morgan is not sure about the paragraph on salt taxes, so Morgan selects it, chooses Comment, and leaves a note in the margin. Too much arithmetic? The note belongs to the folio, and travels with it. Ask an editor brings a particular voice into the thread, and Monsieur Le Stylo arrives with an opinion.",

-      "Selecting a marker unfolds its thread beside the manuscript. Morgan replies, asks another editor, or resolves it. One conversation holds the foreground at a time, and Escape closes it. A reply Morgan has not sent survives switching threads, but not a reload. Send it, or lose it.",
-      "The 1911 survey. The tide table. The book Morgan keeps paraphrasing. The Apparatus keeps them in order.",

-      "Morgan does not ask for sources. A short while after the typing stops, the Apparatus reads the draft and picks out what a careful reader would want backed up: a figure about the salt trade, a line quoted from the survey, the year the harbour closed. It searches for each one, and files what it finds under the claim that prompted it.",

-      "The panel always says what it is doing, or why it is waiting. Every claim explains its result. Found means there are sources on file, so Morgan checks that they support the wording. No match means the search ran and came back empty; perhaps the sentence needs softer wording. Failed means the search broke, which is not the same thing, and Twyne tries again on its own.",

-      "References gather as Morgan writes: links, book numbers, author and year. Morgan saves what matters to the bibliography, in MLA, APA or Chicago, and switches styles the moment an editor changes their mind.",

-      "Morgan signs in with Not Organic, so the account, the hosted credit and the plan come along to every device. The editors address Morgan by name; the email address stays in private settings. Anyone can keep writing locally without signing in at all.",

-      "From one of Le Lecteur's notes, Morgan chooses Talk, and the voice desk opens. Live shows captions, lets Morgan mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose edits in the middle of the conversation. A proposed edit waits for Morgan's approval before it touches the manuscript. Neither the captions nor the audio are kept. The desk shows its spending limits before the conversation starts, which is why Morgan reads them.",
-      "Salt Roads needs a table of caravan stages, a footnote, and one pull quote set just so.",

-      "Morgan types a slash at the start of a line, and the insert menu opens. The outline jumps between headings, and dragging a heading moves its whole section in one edit. Find and Replace understands whole words and patterns.",

-      "The table gets a caption and a little shading. A photograph of the salt flats goes in with a caption and a description for readers who cannot see it. Footnotes are written beside the words they belong to, and equations render on the device.",

-      "When the page is not enough, there is the source underneath it. The Typst workspace shows the source on one side and a paginated proof on the other. A draft that does not compile is never applied. It waits there to be fixed.",
-      "Salt Roads, its outline, and a scratch file of cut paragraphs share a collection, and nothing else. Each is its own folio, with its own dossier, word count and layout.",

-      "Twyne keeps checkpoints on its own as Morgan writes. A week into the revision, Morgan opens Version history and compares today with Monday. The comparison describes itself in a sentence. Rewrote three passages and cut one. The changes reach passages Monsieur Le Stylo had notes on. Each passage shows its before and after, and where a rewrite reached an editor's note, the note sits beside it. That shows the change reached the passage. Whether it answered the note is for Morgan to judge.",
-      "Before a risky pass, Morgan saves a checkpoint and writes what it is for: pay off the ledger promise. Restoring an earlier version always saves the current draft first.",

-      "When the essay is done, Morgan exports a PDF, typeset on the device, with the private editorial notes left out. Share publishes a page anyone with the link can read, and publishing to a personal data server files the essay in Morgan's own repository. Unpublishing takes it down at once.",
-      "Morgan already pays for a model, and would like the editors to use it. It takes three steps, once.",

-      "In Preferences, Morgan switches on Bring Your Own Key and adds a provider: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or any service that speaks the OpenAI format, with its address. Test key checks that the key reaches the list of models. Then a grid assigns a model to each job: the expensive one where the reading matters, something cheaper for the rest.",
-      "If the provider goes down, the desk keeps working. Only the editors go quiet.",
-      "Salt Roads belongs to Morgan. Here is exactly where it goes.",

-      "The drafts live in Morgan's browser. Signing out does not erase them, and signing in is what carries them to another device. Keys live in the browser too. A request with Morgan's own key passes through Twyne's relay to the chosen provider, and the relay keeps neither the key nor the request. A model running on Morgan's own machine is called directly.",

-      "When an editor reads, the draft goes to whichever model is doing the reading. Hosted readings go through Twyne's service and Not Organic. And nothing becomes public until Morgan publishes it. An essay about salt roads is nobody's business until Morgan says it is.",

Recipe that worked on 2026-10-17 for verifying editor UI changes without the Convex backend:

- **Port:** 5173 may belong to another project (interleave-app). Start twyne with `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 bun run dev.frontend`.

Instead, seed like `e2e/instruments.e2e.ts` `seed()`: route `/api/auth/` to `null`, visit a routed blank page, `import("/src/utils/idb.ts")` in page context, then call saveFoliosToIdb / saveFolioContentToIdb / saveActiveFolioIdToIdb (+ `signin-toast-dismissed` meta, `twyne:editor:view:v1` with zenMode false).
- **T3 preview tool:** its viewport can be zoomed or scaled (innerWidth ≠ the requested size), and evaluate/snapshot time out on heavy pages. Prefer the headless script for measurements.
- **Known flaky pair (pre-existing at HEAD bfa07af1):** `struggle-tracker.test.ts` and `quick-review.test.ts` fail together in one bun run (shared System One budget state). Each passes alone. Don't blame new changes for it.
- **Running e2e:** with the dev server on 5174, `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 npx playwright test <file>` works.
  - Screenshot suites (instruments, instrument-dock, instrument-room, living-desk) must run under `--config playwright.visual.config.ts`. It starts its own server on 5187 and compares against the committed `e2e/visual-baselines/`. The default config writes stray `e2e/*-snapshots/` folders; delete them afterwards.
  - About 38 default-config e2e tests already failed at HEAD bfa07af1 (checked on 2026-10-17 against a clean worktree). The causes:

    - Tests expect a visible `.twyne-toolbar`, Bold, or read-aloud control, but zen is now the default and those sit in the collapsed Compositor. This breaks __responsive, select-all and read-aloud.

- **Qwik gotcha:** a component inside a closed `<details>` never runs its `useVisibleTask$` (it has no box). Mount it only while the disclosure is open.

Each manual chapter can now be heard. A **Listen** control under each chapter's lead plays a narration that tells that chapter as Morgan's story. Chapters 01 to 15 are voiced, about 20 minutes in total; Shortcuts and the launch-film section are not. I tested it in a headless browser: playback, the transcript following along, seeking, moving on to the next chapter, and films pausing the narration all work, with no console errors. Nothing is committed.

**What it sounds like.** Each narration is a short story, not a reading of the page. "Morgan Vale has four thousand words about salt caravans, and no idea what the essay is for…" Morgan writes the dossier answers, gets the "unpaid promise" card about the ledger, marks Mademoiselle Sceptique's note as intentional, and reads the "Rewrote three passages" summary in Version history. Each one covers the same controls and the automatic behaviour as its written chapter. The voice is the launch films' narrator, so the films and the manual sound like one production.

**How it behaves:**
- **One press plays through to the end.** When a chapter finishes, the next one starts, and the page scrolls to it if you were following along.
- **A transcript under each control** marks the paragraph being read; select any paragraph to listen from there.
- **Lock-screen and media keys** show the chapter title and can skip between chapters.
- **A film starting pauses the narration.** Switching tabs or following a contents link doesn't, so you can keep listening while reading elsewhere.
- **Visitors need no account or AI provider, and pay nothing.** The audio is rendered ahead of time.
- **Printing leaves the controls out.**

**How I checked the audio.** I can't listen to it, so I transcribed every paragraph back and compared it with the script. Nothing was dropped, repeated or invented. The only differences were numerals, the French editor names spelled phonetically by an English transcriber, and one mishearing. Two lines didn't work aloud, so I reworded and re-rendered them:
- "Yusuf / Yousef": the two spellings sound identical, so the typo couldn't be heard.
- "got a B": transcribed as "gotta be".

**Where things live:**
- **Scripts:** `src/routes/docs/manual-narration-script.ts`. Edit a paragraph there, then run `bun scripts/gen-manual-narration.ts`. It re-renders only the chapters that changed, through fal using the key in skate.
- **Audio:** `public/assets/manual/narration/`, 6.9 MB, committed alongside the films.
- **Test:** `manual-narration.test.ts` fails if a script's wording no longer matches its audio, if chapters are out of order, or if the narration uses a gendered pronoun for Morgan.
- **Docs:** I documented the setup in `docs/manual-visuals.md` and added a line to the manual's introduction.

**One wording correction.** In my earlier docs update I used "Marguerite" in two places. That's an editor staged for a screenshot, not one of the five resident editors, so I changed them to Professeur Athenæum and M. Le Stylo.

Typecheck and the narration tests pass. I didn't run the full test suite.

# Deploying Twyne

Twyne ships as a Qwik City SSR app. The browser bundle is built by Vite into
`dist/`, the SSR server entry into `server/`, and `server.js` (Node `http`)
serves both and listens on `$PORT`.

## Railway (primary)

The repo is configured for [Railway](https://railway.com) via `railway.json`
(`builder: RAILPACK`) and [`railpack.json`](https://railpack.com) — Railpack is
Railway's successor to Nixpacks:

- **Install** (Bun): `bun install --frozen-lockfile`
- **Build** (Bun): `bash scripts/railway-build.sh` — runs Convex deploy + Vite
  client + Vite SSR server. If `CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY` is unset, the script
  degrades to a frontend-only build (backend left untouched).
- **Start** (Node): `node server.js`
- **Healthcheck**: `GET /`

> The `build` step is auto-generated by Railpack from the Node provider
> (uses the mise step to install `bun` + `node`, then runs
> `bun install --frozen-lockfile`). We only override the `build` step to
> inject the Convex deploy + Vite build via `scripts/railway-build.sh` —
> the script is required because the inline `if/then/else` with nested
> single-quoted `&&` strings gets mangled by the build step's shell
> serialization.

`railpack.json` pins `node: 20` + `bun: 1` so the runtime image has `node`
available for the start command (`server.js` uses `node:http`), while Bun does
the install and Vite build.

### One-time setup

1. **Create / link the service** (already linked to `Diogenesoftoronto/twyne`):

   ```bash
   railway add --service twyne --repo Diogenesoftoronto/twyne
   ```

   Railway auto-deploys on every push to the connected branch.

2. **Set environment variables** (see `.env.example` for the full list). The
   `VITE_*` values are baked in at build time, so they must be set on the
   service before the first build:

   ```bash
   railway variables \
     --set "CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY=prod:your-deployment|..." \
     --set "VITE_CONVEX_URL=https://your-deployment.convex.cloud" \
     --set "VITE_CONVEX_SITE_URL=https://your-deployment.convex.site" \
     --set "BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=..." \
     --set "BETTER_AUTH_URL=https://www.twyne.love" \
     --set "SITE_URL=https://www.twyne.love"
   ```

   `CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY` is the production **deploy key** from the Convex
   dashboard (Settings → Deploy keys). The build step uses it to push the
   backend; without it the build only ships the frontend. `PORT` is injected by
   Railway automatically — do not set it.

3. **Custom domain**: in the Railway service → Settings → Networking, add
   `www.twyne.love` and point the DNS `CNAME` at the generated Railway target.
   Until the domain resolves, auth callbacks that expect `https://www.twyne.love`
   will not complete — use the `*.up.railway.app` URL or temporarily set
   `BETTER_AUTH_URL`/`SITE_URL` to it while testing.

### Convex in production

`VITE_CONVEX_URL` should point at a **production** Convex deployment, not a dev
one. The Railway build now runs `npx convex deploy` (gated on `CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY`)
as part of the build step, so the backend deploys on every push alongside the
frontend — no separate manual deploy needed.

Sign-in is through Not Organic. ATProto is a separate publishing connection;
Twyne’s email-code and passkey routes are retired. Register each public sign-in
origin with Not Organic, including its `/auth/notorganic/` callback.

Server-side Convex secrets (`NOTORGANIC_ASSERTION_PRIVATE_KEY`,
`NOTORGANIC_ASSERTION_KEY_ID`, `NOTORGANIC_ENABLED`,
`NOTORGANIC_TWYNE_PRO_V2_ENABLED`, `POSTHOG_PROJECT_API_KEY`,

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Railway build step: deploy Convex backend (when key is configured), then
# build the Qwik City frontend + SSR server.
#
# Gating: when CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY is unset (frontend-only deploys, preview
# environments, local re-runs) we still build the frontend but skip the
# backend push.

set -euo pipefail

if [ -n "${CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY:-}" ]; then
  echo "==> Deploying Convex backend"
  # 1.46 fixes index-removal review with deploy-only keys. Keep CI deployment
  # tooling explicit even when the app's lockfile pins an older client.
  npx --yes convex@1.46.0 deploy --cmd 'bun run build.client && bun run build.server'
else
  echo "==> CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY not set — building frontend only, skipping convex deploy"
  bun run build.client
  bun run build.server
fi

+- **The editors read on their own.** Once **200 words** are new or rewritten
+  since their last reading _and_ you have paused for **a minute**, all five
+  editors read the changed paragraphs, plus a digest of how the draft has been
+  moving. Rewrites count as much as new material. A folio they have never read
+  is read on its own once it reaches 500 words. What they last read is kept
+  per folio, so reopening a folio that already has notes stays quiet. Spend
+  guards: five minutes between passes and eight passes a session. Turn it off
+  with **Read as I write** in the room settings.
+- **Quotations lead to passages.** Every passage an editor quotes in a note or
+  reply links to the sentence it came from. Matching is literal: typography,
+  case and spacing are normalised, `…` elisions are followed within one
+  paragraph, and the note's own words choose between repeated phrases. A

+  says why. Links are re-checked whenever the draft changes.

+  that editor will not raise the same passage again until its text changes.
+  The decisions go to the editors as context too.

+  says why research is idle: waiting for a pause, draft too short, no claims,

Let the editors, research and grade act without being asked

Twyne now does its editorial work on its own; the buttons stay as shortcuts.

- The background room reads a folio it has never seen once it reaches 500
  words, and reads again after 200 new or rewritten words and a minute's
  pause. What it last read is kept per folio.
- After each quick grade the editors read the new version in the
  background, at most every ten minutes, and their notes survive later
  quick checks, marked when they concern an earlier version.
- Hosted writers without their own model get automatic research: rules
  propose claims and Jev confirms which need a source. Each idle state is
  named, and failed passes retry on their own.
- Every quotation in an editor's note links to its own passage by literal,
  context-aware matching, and stays unlinked rather than guess.
- Echo cards name the relationship between two passages and let the writer
  accept or decline the reading.
- Notes can be marked intentional or later; the same editor will not raise
  that passage again until its text changes.
- Version history describes each comparison, pairs before and after text,
  shows notes a rewrite reached, and records an optional intent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
